articleTitle: Frequency-Fresnel Domain Equalization for Underwater Acoustic OCDM Systems
abstract: Orthogonal Chirp Division Multiplexing (OCDM) is a promising multi-carrier modulation for Underwater Acoustic (UWA) systems, as several low complexity OCDM receivers capable of exploiting the channel diversity have already been proposed. However, OCDM receivers are often designed and studied over time-invariant channels. This paper proposes a hybrid Frequency-Fresnel domain equal-izer to enhance the system performance over the doubly selective UWA channel. Our method first estimates the Channel Impulse Response (CIR) using pilot blocks and the Least Square (LS) criterion. The CIR is then sparsified by removing coefficients below a threshold, and the receiver performs equalization in the frequency domain. To address residual InterSymbol Interference (ISI) in doubly selective UWA channels, we propose to equalize again the obtained symbols in the Fresnel domain and perform jointly phase synchronization. Simulations both on synthetic channels and a real underwater channel show that the proposed algorithm improves significantly the BER performance compared to existing methods.

articleTitle: Ocean Flow Observation from Inter – Platform Measurement for Lagrangian Floats
abstract: This paper presents a novel algorithm for estimating the horizontal flow field using inter-platform measurements of displacement among Lagrangian float systems. The primary application of this algorithm is to enhance the navigational perception of Lagrangian floats. The proposed algorithm is grounded in a piecewise linear approximation, with coefficients estimated using an extended Kalman filter. The effectiveness of the algorithm is validated through numerical simulations and tested with data collected from an open sea trial in the Pacific Ocean. The results demonstrate a method for the accurate real time flow field estimations, providing valuable insights for oceanographic research and long-duration ocean monitoring.

articleTitle: Conceptual Design of Autonomous Underwater Walking Robot for Mine Hunting
abstract: Underwater vehicles are becoming the alternatives of the traditional way of mine searching based on Mine Hunter Coastal (MHC) or Mine Sweeper Hunter (MSH). The floating vehicles, however, fundamentally have difficulties to operate in strong current and turbid water area. A hexapod underwater walking robot CRM is proposed for mine hunting in sea-current, turbid, rocky, and burying area. We designed the CRM by extending and adapting the Crabster technologies to the operational concept of mine hunting. The operational concept, functional requirements and conceptual design of CRM are presented in this paper. The focus is on the designing the operating concept and robot platform.

articleTitle: Power Absorption in Oscillatory Flows: Experimental Setup and Preliminary Results
abstract: Ocean wave energy conversion (WEC) has been the subject of research since the oil crisis of the 1970s. A popular wave energy device is the Oscillating Water Column (OWC), which involves very few moving parts. The OWC generates power by guiding ocean waves into a chamber and harnessing the energy of the resulting pulsating flow. In the OWC, the low-frequency wave oscillation is forced through a pneumatic nozzle which accelerates the flow to higher speeds, resulting in better impedance matching with an air turbine connected to an electrical generator. For efficient energy extraction, it is useful to understand the interaction among the various subsystems - hydrodynamics, pneumatics, turbine dynamics, and electrical systems. The power take-off (PTO) of a WEC is one of the most important features as it characterizes the conversion of energy from hydro to pneumatic to mechanical, and then to electrical power. Investigation of the PTO is difficult to perform analytically, and experimental studies are needed for verifying and validating numerical computations. Clearly, it is most cost-effective to perform experiments on small-scale models for data gathering and testing design elements before deploying full-scale prototypes. Small-scale testing is challenging as the different contributing features-hydrodynamics (wave dynamics), mechanical systems (turbine performance), and electrical conversion-scale differently with size variations. Turbines have their own scaling laws, and for simplicity of analysis or experimentation, a porous membrane or orifice plate is used to simulate a linear or nonlinear turbine, respectively. The overarching goal of this study is to build and utilize an oscillatory piston rig to examine damping, simulating the turbogenerator at small scales. The current study employs porous membranes and orifice plates to compare and contrast their features as PTO components. A key objective is to examine the piston amplitude and frequency in response to the input wave signal and measure the corresponding phase lag between the pressure and flow rate across the various dampers. Preliminary results indicate that orifice plates experience higher pressure drops compared to porous plugs in the range of chosen parameters. Such knowledge is critical for developing better scaled model damping proxies for PTO in oscillatory flows, ultimately leading to improved OWC converters.

articleTitle: The Science of Underwater Sound: A Tool for Teaching STEM
abstract: The Discovery of Sound in the Sea (DOSITS) project contributes to and advances the understanding of underwater sound, including how sound behaves underwater, how marine animals produce and receive sound, and what the potential impacts of underwater sound may be. By synthesizing and making available the results of ocean acoustics research for a diverse audience of stakeholders and the public, people in countries around the word have been introduced to the latest knowledge in the field. DOSITS resources address the fundamental understanding of the physics and biology related to underwater sound, as well as advanced scientific content needed by the decision-making community.

articleTitle: Clustered Grasp Volumes for Improved Grasp Selection
abstract: Successful manipulation of objects in unstructured scenes requires identifying an achievable grasp given current environmental conditions. Selecting this grasp is a challenging problem, made more difficult when operating in adversarial conditions. Existing approaches often treat the grasp selection and subsequent path and motion planning as separate optimization tasks which require assuming a static environment. We propose a grasp selection algorithm that clusters grasps by pose and cost to generate discrete graspable volumes. Grasps are chosen from within each cluster by a cost function to maximize visibility of the target and manipulability of the robotic arm. This optimization framework is flexible and allows for autonomous or human-in-the-loop supervision in achieving a grasp through a closed-loop control process. Our approach is evaluated in simulation and in a test tank with a Reach Robotics Bravo 7 robotic arm. Code is available at https://gitlab.com/apl-ocean-engineering/raven/manipulation.

articleTitle: North Atlantic Right Whale (NARW) Line-Array Beamformer Performance Using Energy Detection and Pitch-Tracking Classification Metrics
abstract: A pitch-track classifier is applied to sonar data to detect Right whale upcalls. Data is beamformed and retested. Results fail to demonstrate performance gains. Simulation data is generated to investigate the problem. Variance of the distribution underlying the Mahalanobis distance or classification catalogue is found to be the largest contributor to classifier performance.

articleTitle: Development of an Electric Robotic Arm for the Hadal Zone
abstract: In this paper, we address the challenge of autonomous sampling in ultra-deep water, developing the hadal electric robotic arm. The prototyped three Degree of Freedom (3-DOF) robotic arm uses a newly developed full-ocean depth electric servo motor with a position control based on acceleration feed-forward. This method of Fers a light-weight and disturbance-resistant underwater robot arm even for hadal zone application. The experiment out of water and in the hydrostatic pressure tank shows the last deviation between the desired and feedback position was 0.1%. In ultradeep sea trials, the hadal robotic arm successfully reaches the target positions by an automatic control. Through these experiments, we confirmed that automatic sampling using the robot arm in the hadal zone is feasible.

articleTitle: Toward Energy-Efficient Navigation: A Data-Driven Approach for Flowmeterless Estimation of Ship's Engine Fuel Consumption in Real-Time
abstract: Reducing greenhouse gas emissions from ships is a significant challenge facing the maritime industry. In particular, energy-efficient navigation techniques allow shipowners to adapt their itineraries to minimize fuel consumption. However, the evaluation of the effectiveness of these techniques is slowed down by lack of data on the actual consumption of the engines. Direct measurement of fuel using a flowmeter seems an ideal solution to this problem. However, many shipowners do not adopt it since it requires significant modifications to the fuel inlet piping, reducing ships reliability and requiring significant initial investments. This paper proposes a new, less invasive, data-driven approach to estimating the real-time fuel consumption of engines without using a flowmeter on each ship or each engine of a fleet. The strategy is based on a lookup table fitted in a three-dimensional space composed of torque, rotational speed, and flow measurements gathered on real ships. The model is trained and validated with approximately 464 hours of actual measurements on tugboats operating in North American waters over the last five years. The developed model enables shipowners to evaluate at a low cost the effectiveness of operational measures to reduce their fuel consumption.

articleTitle: Requirement Study on a Specialized Hyperspectral Aerial Imaging System for Marine Plastic Litter Classification
abstract: This paper presents the predesign research for an affordable hyperspectral aerial measurement system for short wave infrared wavelengths. It is shown which design specifications need to be considered and a solution approach for aircraft related tradeoffs is presented, as well as an assessment for data quality and system design parameters for material classification for maritime plastic litter. It is presented that an affordable approach for broad aerial monitoring methods with hyperspectral technology can succeed from a technical point of view. To quantify required data quality, laboratory generated data are used, artificially impaired and analyzed in terms of acceptable noise impairment. Findings as to how high the noise impairment can be for expected classification results of the chosen plastic litter materials are given.

articleTitle: Oxygen Optode Profiles - A Closer Look on Facts and Artefacts
abstract: Oxygen optodes have over time replaced the Clark type electrode oxygen sensors in many instances. This article will look into the performance of one type of these optodes over more than ten years of intermittent use in a profiling mooring in the Baltic Sea. We take a look at the signal processing and the calibration coefficients and the long term signal drift of a JFE Alec Rinko III optode sensor that has been in water with intermissions for a total of 696 days over a span of 13.5 years, mostly in anoxic waters at a depth of around 180 to 200 m. The temporal response of the sensor is evaluated and the reconstruction of the “true” dissolved oxygen concentration from the measurements is discussed.

articleTitle: A Receiver Array to Reduce the Effects of Misalignment in Magneto-Inductive Communication
abstract: In this paper, a magneto-inductive (MI) communication link is designed to cross the air-water interface for a transmitter that is 20 meters below the surface. Simulations are used to identify the geometry of the coils, as well as an optimal transmit frequency on the order of 1 kHz, constrained on a relatively low transmit current of one A RMS. At this frequency, it is shown that the capacity is equal to 5,820 bps, due to the extremely high SNR, over 50 dB. The performance varies significantly with the distance, because the MI link operates in the near field and the bandwidth is reduced because of the conductivity of seawater. The use of an array is demonstrated to improve the SNR with and without misalignment, and a wideband sensor array is proposed to develop a low-noise link receiver. In fact, a 3-element coil array is proposed, and it is expected that the link will be able to achieve an SNR well above 0 dB for a depth of 20 meters.

articleTitle: Low Bandwidth Control of Swarms in Constrained Environments
abstract: Collaborative autonomous surface vehicles (ASV) could use swarm behaviors to address complex tasks like collectively transiting through narrow passages (e.g., leads in Arctic sea ice, as shown in Fig. 1). Generally, swarming involves large numbers of self-organizing entities that interact through simple rules, ranging from gnats to robots. Collaboration, on the other hand, involves fewer entities with deliberation beyond simple rules. However, collaborating robots could engage in swarm behaviors in response to certain situations.

articleTitle: A Visual Perception Algorithm for AUV Dynamic Docking Based on Variable Markers
abstract: Autonomous Underwater Vehicle (AUV), as a key instrument for ocean exploration, utilizes dynamic docking technology to enable energy replenishment and data transfer among multiple AUVs, thereby extending the mission radius. A critical step in AUV dynamic docking is terminal visual positioning and perception. However, current unchanged markers based on point light sources cannot meet the requirements for perception range and dynamic performance.This paper designs a variable marker based on a line light source, whose emission angle can adaptively change according to the docking distance, thus increasing the sensing range and reducing dead zones. Faced with the issues of reduced brightness and increased noise for variable markers underwater, adaptive image enhancement is achieved by combining algorithm Recursive Least Square (RLS) with the image enhancement algorithm Multi-Scale Retinex with Color Restoration (MSRCR). The straight-line fitting algorithm for layer segmentation, combined with line light source information, effectively improves the success rate of visual perception and addresses the issue of key point loss in motion. This paper conducts visual recognition experiments on variable visual markers underwater, verifying the feasibility and accuracy of the proposed visual perception algorithm.

articleTitle: A New Coral Classification Method Using Speed Sea Scanner-Portable and Deep Learning-Based Point Cloud Semantic Segmentation
abstract: Traditional coral classification methods based on underwater images have many limitations in coral surveys, such as light attenuation, color distortion, and complex backgrounds, which affect their accuracy and reliability. To overcome these challenges, we propose a new coral classification method using Speed Sea Scanner-portable (SSS-P-P) and deep learning-based point cloud semantic segmentation. SSS- P can efficiently acquire high-resolution coral images, and we further build coral point clouds through Structure from Motion (SfM) technology. The point cloud semantic segmentation technology can accurately identify and classify corals and other seafloor features. Experimental results show that this method significantly outperforms traditional image segmentation techniques in coral classification accuracy and detection efficiency, providing strong technical support for the research and protection of coral ecosystems.

articleTitle: Long-Term Wave Properties Around Funafuti, Tuvalu from Satellite Imagery
abstract: The coastal region of island nations is subjected to frequent erosion or accretion and is thus considered vulnerable. Numerical models have been used to investigate and predict coastal environments including coastline changes. However, many Pacific Island Countries (PICs) have narrow and low land areas and global ocean models like ERA-5 do not consider that bathymetry. Therefore, the model data are not enough to analyze wave affects to coastline changes. In this work, we developed a method to extract reliable wavelength and wave direction from optical satellites and validated those parameters with ERA-5. Tuvalu, an atoll nation in the Southwest Pacific, is selected as the study region, and multiple satellite data sets are used in this work, which include medium-resolution Sentinel-2 and Landsat-8/9 images. With detailed wave properties, we analyzed a long-term trend from 2013 to 2023. The results of this study will provide valuable advantages for decision-making by accurate information about the coastal environment.

articleTitle: High Frequency Surface Wave Radar Studies of Inertial Oscillations
abstract: Since its inception almost 70 years ago, high frequency (HF) surface wave radar (SWR) has become ubiquitous in ocean physics research. Validation is an important aspect of this relatively new technology and presents interesting chal-lenges. In situ measurements viz.: current meters and drifters yield, respectively, instantaneous Eulerian and Lagrangian current vectors. In contrast, HFSWR vectors are inherently spatio-temporally averaged, thereby confounding direct comparison with in situ results. An additional challenge is that typical standard deviations and means of current velocities are close. We proposed an approach to validation whereby a wind driven one dimensional inertial oscillation model is fitted to the current meter observations. Model radial velocities are then compared against those of a monostatic radar. We found the radar and model velocities to be highly correlated for several days following the excitation of oscillations by a transient wind event.

articleTitle: Reinforcement Learning for Space-Time Access in MISO Uplink Underwater Acoustic Communications
abstract: Underwater acoustic communication shows unique challenges arising from the complex and dynamic nature of the propagation medium. Traditional approaches to enhance the communication efficiency have often fallen short due to the inherent uncertainties and limitations of underwater channels. Recently, the advances in artificial intelligence offer promising to address these challenges. Specifically, this paper presents an overview of the potential application of reinforcement learning to handle multiple access in underwater acoustic networks exploiting space and time domains. By leveraging reinforcement learning algorithms, autonomous agents can adaptively learn optimal communication strategies in response to changing environmental conditions, improving channel usage and, therefore, data throughput, reliability, and energy efficiency.

articleTitle: Building an Agile Ocean Technician Workforce for Today and Tomorrow
abstract: Globally, the needs and requirements of marine technicians from decades past are significantly different from the skills and competencies of today's workforce. In the past, the typical “technician” for the industry came from trade focused skills including electronics and hydraulics or a technical trade focused two-year associates degrees from community colleges. Supporting today's technical marine based workforce requires agile approaches and a shift from traditional knowledge transfer to a competency-based approach that needs to adapt to diverse learner profiles and backgrounds.

articleTitle: Deployment of a Solar-Powered Field Camera for Monitoring Living Marine Resources
abstract: Monitoring of living marine resources in their natural habitats can be done with a solar-powered and computer-based field camera system designed and assembled using commercially available components. River herring are ecologically, and socioeconomically, significant to the North American Atlantic Coast. They are anadromous forage fish that return to inland freshwater ecosystems to spawn every spring and are a key component of the energy transfer between marine and freshwater ecosystems. River herring, as forage fishes, support many recreational and commercial fish species and the associated fisheries. River herring populations have declined compared to historic levels due to decades of habitat loss and degradation, overfishing, and as bycatch in other Atlantic fisheries. They have supported some of the oldest fisheries in North America, and to this day the Mashpee Wampanoag tribe relies on the river herring as a food source. The annual river herring spawning runs support local ecotourism and community connection to natural resources, despite a moratorium on harvest in the state of Massachusetts. Local and state fisheries managers, scientists, and conservation groups are collaborating to restore river herring habitats and populations, which are monitored with human observers and electronic counting systems. Additional methodologies for population estimation are needed to better understand population dynamics over time and between locations. A video surveillance system can economically observe and record the spawning migration for later review, archiving, or sharing/outreach. Solar-powered field cameras were installed in the Santuit River and the Coonamessett River on Cape Cod, Massachusetts, USA to monitor the river herring spawning populations. The cameras have infrared lights for nighttime recording, and the computer controlling it was set to record 24 hours per day; storing the footage locally in an external solid-state drive as (24) 1 hour-long videos. Video footage of the spawning migration can be reviewed by humans or paired with computer-based image recognition technologies. The “HelioCase” is a portable, solar-battery-powered, Raspberry Pi-based system that was developed by Bennett et al, 2023. The HelioCase is intended to be an economic and robust field computer system that can be easily customized to fit user needs, in this scenario it acts as a remote field camera for marine wildlife observation. Power is supplied by solar panels and is stored in a lightweight LiFePO4 battery. The Raspberry Pi acts as the camera controller unit and access point. The Raspberry Pi computer can utilize cellular or satellite networks for internet access and remote control; data transmission and camera control can be done remotely or locally. This deployment of the HelioCase system aims to improve population estimates through more complete monitoring of the annual spawning migration event, providing river herring monitoring coverage for the times of the day that human observers are not present. This paper discusses the construction of the HelioCase with commercially available components, and the deployment in two rivers on Cape Cod that support river herring populations. Consumer camera and computer technology is an accessible method for natural resource managers to monitor multiple points of interest and can promote more efficient and effective decision-making for sustaining valuable living marine resources.

articleTitle: A Machine Learning Approach to Modeling Small Vessel Performance
abstract: The maritime industry is a critical component of global trade. However, it is also responsible for a significant amount of Greenhouse Gas emissions. While small vessels are often overlooked as main contributors to emissions, when analyzed as a group, they collectively have a meaningful impact. In order to help promote more sustainable operation of these vessels, it is important to to model fuel consumption based on different weather and sea conditions. To this end, we present a machine learning approach to modelling fuel consumption aboard small vessels using an LSTM architecture. In this paper, we discuss the process of collecting data aboard one such small vessel, the end-to-end model training & evaluation process, and discuss plans for future work.

articleTitle: Underwater Instrumentation Deployment Using a Small Remotely Operated Vehicle
abstract: Advances in underwater sensing technology have resulted in the reduction of the size and cost of instrumentation packages. As a result, sensing systems can be deployed in larger numbers, increasing the spatial resolution of measurements, providing a better picture of the underwater landscape as it relates to a particular sensing modality. In addition, minimization trends in electronics have reduced power consumption requirements which, coupled with advances in battery technology, has increased the functional lifetime of many systems. This also impacts memory, which has notably increased in storage size while dropping in price, enabling for more frequent measurements, increasing temporal resolution. The reduction in the size and increases in capabilities of underwater instrumentation paves the way for more accessible, intentional, targeted deployment of systems. This paper addresses the deployment of such instruments using mini class remotely operated vehicles (ROV s) including: 1) the design, implementation, and testing of a payload release mechanism, 2) consideration of recovery mechanisms on deployment, and 3) ballasting and trim of a payload/ROY coupled system. Deployment is demonstrated with a payload of an underwater camera with integrated temperature and depth sensors with communication provided by an acoustic modem.

articleTitle: Ship Matching Issues Using AIS and Satellite Radio Frequency Data
abstract: Satellite remote sensing data identifies vessels that either don't transmit Automatic Identification System (AIS) signals or provide incorrect coordinates., while radio frequency (RF) satellite data effectively monitors ships that disable AIS or Vessel Monitoring System (VMS) devices. Unseenlabs of Fers RF data for X- and S-bands., but their matching results with AIS data have limitations that can lead to incorrect ship identification. This study addresses the issues in Unseenlabs” matching results and proposes a matching algorithm based on a distance for RF and AIS data in the Yellow Sea. In the overlapping region of RF and AIS data., the matching rate varied from 80.2 % to 98.7%., with an average of 89.3%., and no duplicate matches were observed. The study's findings reveal the RF and AIS matching rate., of Fering key insights for future multi-dataset ship identification research.

articleTitle: Examining the Capability of Machine Learning Methods for Unraveling Ocean Dynamics from Long-Range M-Sequence Data
abstract: Accurately representing ocean dynamics is crucial for naval monitoring and has garnered significant interest. The complexity of the ocean, akin to other intricate physical systems, poses challenges due to the absence of a closed-form equation of the dynamics. Additionally, environmental nonlinearities further complicate modeling efforts. However, recent advancements in data-driven machine learning methods offer promising solutions for unraveling some of the complex patterns in the ocean. In this work, we use long range m-sequence waveform data to investigate the ocean's hidden dynamics. The methods employed are inherently data-driven, enabling the discovery of low dimensional representations of the data without supervision. Preliminary results from applying these methods to m-sequence waveform data from the Wake Island Station are presented.

articleTitle: Experimental Investigations of an Elastic- Membrane Integrated Oscillating Water Column Wave Energy Converter
abstract: In light of the adverse environmental impact of fossil fuels, transition to cleaner renewable energy resources is currently underway. The present research aims to contribute to the development of ocean wave energy converter (WEC) technology as a sustainable energy source. To achieve this goal, the objective of this work is to improve the efficiency of an oscillating water column (OWC) wave energy converter design by increasing the frequency bandwidth of power capture. To accomplish the bandwidth improvement, one option is to add another component to the traditional OWC with its own resonance characteristics. An integrated design of the elastic membrane with the conventional OWC (e-OWC) can potentially enhance the range of power capture across the bandwidth of wave frequencies. In our experiments, we use a rubber membrane as the new component to tune the natural frequency by adjusting its geometry and material properties. This study analyzes the experimental integration of the rubber membrane into a model-scale OWC device, exploring the elastic properties required to achieve the desired natural frequency alignment with full-scale wave characteristics. The investigation comprises two sets of experiments. The first set is the traditional standalone OWC and the second is the OWC integrated with a rubber membrane, the e-OWC. This allows for a comparison between the two designs to investigate changes in frequency response. The main contribution of the paper is the damped frequency response of the OWC compared with the e-OWC. It is shown that the e-OWC enhances the CWR at resonance. Therefore, the inclusion of a well-designed elastic membrane proves to increase the efficiency of the OW C approach to wave energy conversion.

articleTitle: Computer Vision Based Intelligence for Tracking and Predicting Whale Blow Trajectories
abstract: Collecting blow samples from whales allows for studies on individual and population health. However, it is important to not interfere or harm the whales, forcing collections to happen from a distance. An Uncrewed Aerial Vehicle (UAV) equipped with a collection system is capable of collecting whale blow samples without interfering with the whale by flying through the blow cloud. The work presented describes a computer vision based intelligence system for facilitating whale blow collection using an UAV. The computer vision system utilizing Ultralytics Neural Network You Only Look Once (YOLO) version 8. Using the timing of YOLO's outputs, an averaging technique is used to predict future blow timings from past ones. Additionally, an Auto Regressive Moving Average (ARMA) model is used in combination with the bounding boxes provided by YOLO in order to predict where the blow centres will be in the near future. It is shown that YOLO is able to successfully identify a whale, its head, and the blow while the ARMA model is able to predict where the blow will be sufficient accuracy for collection.

articleTitle: Cerulean Information Factory: A New European Space Agency-Funded Project to Develop Decision-Support Tools for the North Atlantic and Arctic Oceans
abstract: The The European Space Agency (ESA), responding to the European Green Deal-Europe's commitment to climate neutrality by 2050-has launched the Green Transition Information Factory (GTIF) program. Its goal is to use satellite and other data to create tools for decision-makers to support the transition to a greener economy. “The ESA Green Transition Information Factory (GTIF) allows users to interactively discover the underlying opportunities and complexities of transitioning to carbon neutrality by 2050 using the power of Earth Observation, cloud-computing and cutting-edge analytics.” - ESA The Green Economy is “one that results in improved human well-being and social equity, while significantly reducing environmental risks and ecological scarcities” (United Nations). The Blue Economy refers to “sustainable use of ocean resources for economic growth, improved livelihoods and jobs, and ocean ecosystem health.” (World Bank). Since the oceans are part of all natural cycles and, directly or indirectly, involved in all economic sectors, there cannot be a Green Transition without the blue component. ESA is sponsoring a GTIF that addresses a green transition for the blue economy named the Cerulean Information Factory (CIF) after the blue-green colour and reflecting the need to connect the Blue and Green Economies in order to have a successful Green Transition. The focus of the project, launched in Spring of 2024, will be on the North Atlantic and Arctic oceans between Canada and Europe. The initial capabilities will focus on three domains: 1.offshore Renewable Energy: Integrating multiple data sources to provide user-definable metrics for offshore renewable energy potential and risk for offshore renewable energy, including solar, tidal, wave, wind and current energy. Analytical capabilities will include: •energy potential of sites; •accessibility of sites, including water depth, and distance to shore and energy markets; •vulnerability of sites to adverse environmental conditions, including sea ice, icebergs, and extreme waves and winds; and, •forecasts for winds, sea ice, waves and currents. 2.Ship Carbon Intensity Minimisation and Arctic Accessibility: Providing a route optimization tool for vessels in ice that minimises fuel consumption, ship emissions, and travel time, while maintaining ship safety in sea ice and icebergs. This capability will provide a tool to support both: •Ship operators with voyage planning, and, •Policymakers in evaluating the impact of the International Maritime Organization's Carbon Intensity Indicator (CII) regulation and future changes in the accessibility of Arctic regions due to climate change. 3.Aquaculture: Providing indicators of ocean health and potential risks for aquaculture sites by enabling end-users to filter and combine ocean and meteorological observations and forecasts. This capability will support: •Assessment of aquaculture site suitability based on historical water quality and presence of microorganisms, such as temperatures and nutrients, and, •Early warning systems, such as harmful algal blooms, pollution and eutrophication. Throughout the project, the CIF team will be engaging with end users to identify requirements and co-develop the tools that decision-makers in industry, government and civil society need; transforming ocean data into information for decision making. The project team is made up of a consortium of organisations with Earth Observation expertise from both sides of the Atlantic Ocean, including Polar View, EOX, Danish Meteorological Institute, C-CORE, and the National Research Council Canada. At OCEANS 2024, we will demonstrate the initial capabilities of the CIF.

articleTitle: Effective Segmentation of X-Band Marine Radar Images Using SegFormer
abstract: X-band marine radar imaging has been widely used for ocean surface monitoring and parameter estimation. However, the quality of radar images can be significantly affected by various meteorological conditions, leading to inaccurate estimation of ocean surface parameters. In this paper, a novel approach is proposed for segmenting X-band marine radar images into four distinct regions using the SegFormer model, an advanced semantic segmentation architecture that employs a hierarchical transformer encoder to capture global context and a lightweight all-multilayer perception (MLP) decoder to enable high-resolution segmentation. The four regions include areas with clear wave signatures, rain-contaminated areas, low backscatter areas, and wind-dominated rain areas. The experimental data collected by a shipborne Decca radar system is used to validate the effectiveness of the proposed method, and a SegNet-based segmentation approach is utilized for comparison. Experimental results demonstrate that the SegFormer-based method outperforms the SegNet-based method, with an improvement of 0.5% in mean segmentation accuracy.

articleTitle: Enhancing the Positional Accuracy of Merged Regional Acoustic Corer Data Sets: A Case Study from an Offshore Wind Farm in the Baltic Sea
abstract: In offshore wind farm (OWF) construction, mitigating the risk of sub-seabed geohazards and investigating the foundation conditions for fixed bottom wind turbine generator (WTG) and offshore substation (OSS) platform locations is of paramount concern. In October 2023, Kraken Robotics carried out a sub-bottom survey using one of our cutting-edge imaging systems, the Acoustic Corer (AC), for an OWF development project in the Baltic Sea. The aim was to assess the conditions of the potential foundation legs for two OSS platforms, each with four legs. This involved interpreting and mapping cobbles and boulders below the seabed. The AC is equipped with low- and high-frequency chirp projectors and a parametric source on each boom that enables data collections spanning from 1.5 kHz to 12.5 kHz (Guigné et al., 2010; Guigné et al., 2012; Guigné & Blondel, 2017). This configuration operates from a stationary landed survey platform. The AC produces a 14 m diameter volumetric dataset, known as an “acoustic core”, down to 60 m below the seabed, depending on soil conditions. For this project, the main objective was to assess the shallow soil conditions for the survey area down to 15 m below the seabed while identifying acoustic responses that are suggestive of the presence of cobbles and boulders 0.2 m in length and width or greater. Kraken Robotics proposed to the client the utilization of the AC triple core application (Abbott et al., 2023). This technique had previously been employed at a proposed wind turbine generator (WTG) site in the Baltic Sea for a similar investigation into the soil conditions of the location, including the interpretation of geohazards, obstructions and stratigraphy. In the triple-core application, three acoustic cores are acquired separately, however they are positioned to partially overlap to provide increased data coverage over the location of interest. Subsequently, all three acoustic cores are merged into a single unified volumetric dataset and corrected laterally and vertically based on a common anomaly detected by each acoustic core, with the support of an ultra-short baseline acoustic positioning system (USBL). This approach integrates all volumetric datasets into a common framework, enabling a more coherent summation of anomalies within that volume. However, shallow water USBL positioning for the OWF survey typically resulted in an uncertainty of ±50 cm due to the shallow water in the survey area. Kraken Robotics devised a new approach to reduce positional uncertainty. A beacon was placed onto the seabed at each triple acoustic core location where all three acoustic cores could capture it. The beacon remained in the same position on the seabed until all three AC data sets were acquired. Subsequently, the beacon response captured by all three acoustic cores is vertically and laterally shifted to the exact location of the beacon during the pre-migration data conditioning. This adjustment, applied to the entire dataset, provided higher confidence towards merging three regional acoustic cores and the lateral and vertical correction of acoustic cores. This was followed by the standard seismic processing steps and three-dimensional (3-D) pre-stack Kirchhoff time migration using Kraken Robotics proprietary signal processing software, ZoomSpace. After processing and interpreting each triple-core, Kraken Robotics successfully reported 1057 anomalies suggestive of cobbles or boulders equal to or greater than 0.2 m in length and width at the two OSS platform legs. Additionally, the AC results were compared and correlated with stratigraphic interpretations obtained from previous geotechnical and geophysical surveys, showcasing that the acoustic cores represented the sediment stratigraphy of the survey area.

articleTitle: Using Ambient Sensor Data to Characterize and Predict Autonomous Perception Sensor Performance
abstract: With the development of low-cost, small Uncrewed Underwater Vehicles (UUVs), the use of cost-efficient sensor systems imposes its own constraints (e.g., sensor accuracy and precision). Such sensors include Mechanically Scanning Imaging Sonars (MSIS), Conductivity-Temperature-Depth (CTD), and Commercial-off-the-Shelf (COTS) stereo camera systems, all of which are widely accessible perception sensors. To accommodate for the disadvantages that these low-cost sensors impose, the authors present a methodology to predict the accuracy and precision of specific perception sensor measurements in practical field implementation by leveraging the redundancy of several common on-board sensors. This insight can then be used to determine UUV region coverage control to allow for an ample collection of data samples (e.g., greater UUV loitering over areas with less-reliable data collection to ensure greater sample quantity and quality). Overall, the aim of this paper is to show how low-cost UUV sensor systems can be implemented without sacrificing sensor performance, particularly when compared to using their more expensive counterparts. This methodology developed by the authors is presented as the Standardized Heuristic Algorithm for Reinforced Calculations (SHARC). Here, the authors use an analytical model to show proof of concept of the validity of this proposed method. To test the SHARC algorithm, this study focuses on modeling a Mechanically Scanning Imaging Sonar (MSIS) in the BELLHOP simulation program and uses historic Sound Velocity Profiles (SVPs) to identify how the MSIS is affected by various ambient surroundings. Results show that the SVP shape affects the MSIS range of the probability of detection. It is observed that a change in SVP slope correlates to a reduced MSIS performance range as opposed to that of a more constant SVP depth profile, which increases the MSIS performance range. The authors show that SHARC enables the use of low-cost sensors to compete with higher capability counterparts by leveraging a priori data analysis to gauge in situ data performance and applies these techniques to a simulated MSIS to validate.

articleTitle: Super-Resolution Approaches Based Shallow-Water Benthic Identification Using Multispectral Satellite Imagery
abstract: Traditional coral reefs monitoring methods based on field surveys, such as line intercept transects or those based on autonomous underwater vehicles (AUVs) or the novel Portable Speedy Sea Scanner (P-SSS), are both costly and labor-intensive, and are not well-suited for long-term monitoring. In contrast, in recent years, an increasing number of studies have utilized multispectral satellite imagery for coral reef monitoring, which are more low-cost, efficient, and well-suited for long-term monitoring. However, the effectiveness of such monitoring is limited by the spatial resolution of satellite images, which leads to the mixed pixel phenomenon. To mitigate the impact of mixed pixels on satellite monitoring, this study introduces a coral reef monitoring working flow based on single image super-resolution (SISR) algorithms and benthic identification algorithm. This working flow enhances the spatial resolution of original satellite images through a SISR reconstruction and performs coral reef detection using the proposed benthic identification algorithm. By comparing drone aerial photography data from field surveys in Ko Tao Island, Thailand, coral reefs identified in images reconstructed with the SISR algorithm showed higher accuracy, from 81.7% to 86.3%, and clearer boundaries, which reduces the impact of mixed pixels on the effectiveness of satellite monitoring.

articleTitle: Operational Concept and Design of Multiple AUVs for Rapid Underwater Investigation in Case of Maritime Accidents
abstract: After a helicopter crash off Dokdo Island in 2019, Korea Coast Guard (KCG) decided to develop an unmanned vehicle system capable of underwater survey even in harsh marine environments. The whole system consists of four small-sized AUVs equipped with side scan sonars (SSS AUVs), a mid-sized AUV with synthetic aperture sonar (SAS AUV), an integrated mission control system (MCS), and sensor data post-processing module (DPP). An unmanned surface vehicle (USV) and a robot buoy (RBB) are also included for real-time monitoring or data transmission with underwater acoustic modems and RF communication systems. Each system design has been completed and manufactured, and performance tests and demonstrations based on scenarios by KCG will be conducted from this year.

articleTitle: EMPC-Based Tracking Control and Energy-Optimal Path Planning for an ASV
abstract: This study explores the use of a robust Explicit Model Predictive Control (EMPC) scheme for an Autonomous Surface Vehicle (ASV). The aim is to manage computational complexity related to online optimization, particularly for fast-response ASVs which are equipped with micro hardware with limited computational capabilities. The optimization process is performed offline a priori to a given mission, and the proposed EMPC scheme is shown to ensure stability via Lyapunov analysis. The authors also investigate the way in which the resulting ASV trajectories, especially taking into account polynomial trajecto-ries, affect the total ASV control effort. This qualitative compari-son of trajectories and respective control efforts is the basis from which ASV control performance is analyzed. Numerical analysis confirms the effectiveness of the proposed EMPC-based control strategies. Additionally, it reveals how energy consumption varies with different polynomial trajectories of varying degrees.

articleTitle: Monitoring Water Reservoirs in Southern Italy and Fighting Water Scarcity
abstract: Water scarcity in Sicily, exacerbated by climate change, irregular rainfall and inefficient waterworks networks, poses significant challenges to the region's water system, particularly affecting agriculture. This paper explores the monitoring and management of Sicilian water reservoirs, highlighting the importance of accurate and timely data. By analyzing water levels and rainfall patterns, sustainable management strategies can be developed to mitigate drought effects. The study emphasizes the use of modern technologies for effective monitoring and provides recommendations for a sustainable water future in Sicily.

articleTitle: Simulation of Sound Propagation Through Random Ice Blocks as an Under-Ice Loss Mechanism
abstract: The propagation of underwater sound waves through a random distribution of ice blocks is studied as a numerical simulation problem. For a sparse distribution of ice blocks, it looks like a scattering problem. For a dense distribution, the blocks of ice are joined to form skeletal frame, and it is a porous medium problem. A range of ice block densities are simulated and compared to provide an insight into the wave propagation speeds and attenuations. The results show a variety of frequency dependencies of both wave speed and attenuation, depending on the acoustic frequency range and ice block density.

articleTitle: Ocean Sound Speed Profile Measurement Using Echo Arrival Times
abstract: In many underwater acoustic applications, knowing the sound speed profile (SSP) is essential because it affects how acoustic signals travel and their strength. Currently, the SSP is measured directly by assessing sound speed or the related parameters of temperature, salinity, and depth. This paper discusses a method for remotely estimating the SSP using underwater acoustics. We introduce a pulse-echo technique that employs a narrow beam directional transmitter and two receivers to determine the sound speed. Our method relies on measuring the travel times of echo signals. Using synthetic signals modeled through a ray tracing approach, we show the effectiveness of our technique. The time of flight for the received signals is calculated using a cross-correlation technique. Comparisons of the estimated SSP with the assumed profile used to generate the synthetic signals confirm our method's accuracy.

articleTitle: A Hybrid ViT-CNN Architecture for Volumetric Target Classification with Sub-Bottom SAS Data
abstract: Deep learning convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have become the state-of-the-art (SOTA) method for automatically classifying targets captured above the seafloor for many 2D synthetic aperture sonar (SAS) imaging systems [1], [2] and recently for targets buried within the sub-bottom [3]–[5]. More specifically, Williams and Brown [3] designed the first 3D CNN architecture to classify objects buried in the sediment. Trung et al. [4] designed neural networks to account for the resonant scattering with volumetric SAS data in shallow water environments. Vetaw et al. [5] introduced a learning-based tone mapping approach to enhance the salient features of buried targets in the sediment while jointly the SOTA 3D CNN model training Williams and Brown [3].

articleTitle: Opearational System to Generate Marine Pollution Information (MPI) Using Satellites, Aircrafts, Drones and Mobile Devices
abstract: Korea Coast Guard (KCG) is operating several types of platforms such as manned and unmanned aircrafts, satellites and smart devices for marine pollution monitoring and surveillance. Korea Institute of Ocean Science and Technology (KIOST) has developed an operational system to generate 5 types of Marine Pollution Information (MPI) for oil spills and some species of floating Hazardous and Noxious Substances (HNS) using multiple platforms. The system, denoted as ISABU (Integrated remote-Sensing Application for oil/f-HNS spill oBservation & evalUation), supports open and commercial SAR and Optical satellites and airplane/drone-based EO video/image and mobile phone. Accuracies of MPI detection exceeds 85% for satellites and 84% for aircrafts, with processing time around 2 minutes for aircraft, PlanetScope, and Landsat, and up to 12 minutes for Sentinel-1/2. An optional function allows experts to evaluate MPIs based on data sources including oceanic and atmospheric environment and ship traffic.

articleTitle: Transparent Oceans: Intelligence for Bering Sea Ecosystems from Interactive Data-Model Fusion
abstract: The Bering Sea is critical for food production and biodiversity: it is home to one of the largest commercial fisheries in the world [1] and it contains habitats for dozens of species that are vulnerable, imperiled, or critically imperiled [2]. However, the Bering Sea is undergoing rapid and pronounced warming [3]–[5] that not only impacts its fisheries [6] and biodiversity, but that also has an outsized impact on the heat distribution around the world [7]. A deeper understanding of the Bering Sea-including its temperature and nutrient distribution, circulation, commercial fish populations, and invasive species-is central to managing and preserving its ecosystem services [8]. To support a deeper understanding, we are executing a project called Transparent Oceans (TO), which aims to create actionable intelligence for ecosystem management by integrating diverse-and often sparse-ocean data and model outputs.

articleTitle: Smart Rope Technology for Aquaculture Farms - Low-Cost Conductive Yarns as Load and Strain Sensors for Integrity Monitoring
abstract: Blue Economy systems like marine energy and aquaculture farms consist of several individual units held by lines made of nylon or fiber ropes. Condition-monitoring of ropes and mooring lines are essential for the overall integrity of a marine energy farm. Our research is aimed at developing a low-cost prototype of a sensor integrated rope that can be used in long-term deployment for comprehensive monitoring purposes. A functional braided composite yarn with integrated electromagnetic properties was integrated into a 5 mm polypropylene rope. Samples with different conductor and core configurations were manufactured by Nautilus Defense. Data processing algorithms for receiving and processing information from the sensors were custom-made and tested at MITRE electronic laboratories. Mechanical tests were conducted at the Ocean Resources and Renewable Energy (ORRE) laboratory at UMass Amherst, where rope samples were subject to varying levels of static and dynamic forcing in dry conditions and under water. The observed linear trend of capacitance with strain offers strong potential for the sensor to support condition monitoring efforts of mooring lines for aquaculture and marine renewable energy.

articleTitle: The Role of Tidal Stream Energy in Green Ammonia and Green Hydrogen Production in The English Channel
abstract: Ammonia and hydrogen production are currently dominated by fossil fuels, which is carbon emissions-intensive. Production of ammonia and hydrogen is also possible with renewable energy, generating no direct carbon emissions. Tidal stream energy is a predictable renewable energy source, and utilising the difference in phase of tidal stream currents in close-by locations can provide a more stable power profile. This stable power profile could be useful as ammonia production has limited flexibility, and although hydrogen production is more flexible, hydrogen storage is particularly expensive. This paper explores the effect of tidal stream phasing on both green ammonia and green hydrogen production in the English Channel for the first time. The coefficient of variation (CV) of the power profiles between pairs of locations is used as a metric of tidal phasing, and the minimum is determined from locations in the English Channel appropriate for an Orbital O2 turbine with a similar energy. This minimum CV method is novel and can be applied to other tidal regions. For 66 MW of Orbital O2 turbines with an average capacity factor 20.5%, utilising phasing reduces the levelized cost of ammonia by 5% and the levelized cost of hydrogen by 4%.

articleTitle: Characterization of the Innomar Deep 36 Sub-Bottom Profiler in the Gulf of Mexico
abstract: A sound source characterization (SSC) of the Innomar Deep-36 sub-bottom profiler was conducted in waters <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim 10\mathbf{m}$</tex> deep in the north western corner of the Gulf of Mexico. Pre-survey modeling assessed the safe distance for very-high frequency mammals exposed to the SBP to be 1100 m. The SSC directly measured the safe distance for marine mammals exposed to the SBP to be 160 m. The SSC assessed several parameters of the Deep-36 and found them to be substantially different than were assumed during pre-survey modeling. The most notable difference was that the beampattern of the Deep-36 is not circular, rather, it is much wider across-track than along track, with broadside sidelobes <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim 26\mathbf{dB}$</tex> higher than those at endfire.

Author Keywords: effects of noise on marine mammals

articleTitle: Distribution of Trace Metals in Seawater from Coastal Areas Near Marine Industrial Facilities and Power Plants
abstract: Hazardous and noxious substances (HNS), when discharged into the marine environment, affect to humans and marine organisms, even corrosive damage to marine facilities, or otherwise interfere with the use of marine areas. Therefore, it is necessary to study the background concentration and distribution status of hazardous substances discharged from marine industrial facilities located along the coast. In this study, a trace metal status survey of HNS in seawater was investigated around 5 industrial facilities and 5 power plants in Korea 2021–2023. Thre result of investigation was Ba, Cr, Cu, Pb, Mn, Zn, As, Cd, Hg, Se, Ni, Sn, Ag and V were detected in all regions and their concentrations were relatively high in some regions. In all regions, the material-specific detection ranges were Ba: 0.58-67.31, Cr: 0.02-19.76, Cu: 0.03-53.46, Pb: 0.0015-7.32, Mn: 0.05-342.12, Zn: 0.33-101.12, As: 0.03-8.68, Cd: 0.0007-0.78, Hg: 0.001-0.01, Se: 0.0044-4.88, Ni: 0.03-4.88, Sn: 0.0025-26.43, Ag: 0.0025-0.87 and V: 0.01-40.71. The aim of this study is to identify and analyse trace metals among HNS present in seawater in the surrounding waters, with the ultimate aim of effectively managing the discharge of HNS in industrial effluents.

articleTitle: Preliminary Evaluation of an AUV Equipped with a Line Laser for Wall Following and Mapping in a Rectangular Tank
abstract: This research studies the feasibility of utilizing an AUV equipped with a line laser for right-side wall following in a rectangular tank and for of Fline wall mapping using laser images and position data, with both aspects preliminarily evaluated through simulations. Methods for locating the AUV relative to the right-side and front walls using laser images are described, alongside a control flow for the wall following mission, which includes both right-side wall following and front wall collision avoidance. In addition, a method for of Fline wall mapping with laser images and position data is outlined. Preliminary simulation results are provided for both right-side wall following and of Fline wall mapping. For wall-following performance, the distance from the AUV's center of gravity to the wall deviates by no more than 0.2 meters from the target value. The AUV's heading relative to the wall's tangential direction deviates by no more than 8° from the target value. For of Fline wall mapping, the estimated dimensions of the rectangular cuboid yield percent errors of 11 %, 5%, and 2% along the X, Y, and Z axes, respectively.

articleTitle: Design, Prototyping, and Experimentation of a Dual Helical Drive Vehicle for Underwater Exploration
abstract: This paper presents the development of a novel underwater screw-propelled vehicle prototype capable of operating both on the surface of the water and underwater. The locomotion of the prototype is controlled by the thrust and buoyancy generated by two helical drives or Archimedes' screws. The thrust generated by the drive depends on its rotational speed while the buoyancy depends on the amount of water in the central cylinder or ballast. Experimentation of the prototype's operation was conducted in a 3.35m-deep diving well at North Carolina State University. Real-time data acquisition and controls were performed through a tethered connection to the vehicle, and video post-processing was used for position estimation. Results from the vehicle's locomotion are presented as it demonstrates a variety of maneuvers including moving along the surface, controlling and maintaining a desired operating depth, and travelling while fully submerged. The experimental data acquired can now be applied towards dynamic model validation in efforts to develop an autonomous underwater screw-propelled vehicle.

articleTitle: Synthetic Sonar Generation: Leveraging Algorithmic and AI-Based Approaches for Enhanced Underwater Mapping and Exploration
abstract: The acquisition of high-quality sonar bathymetry and sidescan imagery is crucial for various underwater applications, including seafloor mapping, habitat characterization, and object detection. However, the collection of such data can be time-consuming, costly, and often limited by environmental and logistical constraints. While synthetic data cannot replace the value of real-world data, it can be a valuable supplement. Specifically, synthetic sonar bathymetry and sidescan imagery can be used to affordably train AI models, facilitate education and training, and enhance the analysis and validation of real data. With these benefits in mind, we propose a novel framework for synthetic generation of sonar bathymetry and sidescan imagery using algorithmic and AI-based tools, which can help augment and support the use of real data in underwater applications.

articleTitle: West Philippine Sea Coral Reef Imagery Using ARRAS Technology
abstract: The Automated Rapid Reef Assessment System (ARRAS), which is a towed platform composed of an underwater camera and echosounder with a stitching algorithm called Kiko&Stitch, were utilized to quantify the coral reef extents of the Kalayaan Island Group (KIG) in the West Philippine Sea (WPS) for its resource valuation where impacts of both natural and anthropogenic activities are investigated. This efficient and inexpensive system allows for optimized sampling specially in cases that require rapid assessments at a limited time frame, a case in point is the WPS where geopolitical tensions are present. Portions of the geotagged stitched images from the captured videos that were classified into corals, seaweed, seagrass, rubble, and sand and extents were assigned as training and validating sets in classifying satellite imagery using semi-automated classification algorithm. This created a habitat map of the KIG reefs validated with a mean accuracy of 0.56. The total calculated area for the 32 identified reef systems in KIG is 3,179 sq km, 40% of which are primarily dominated corals, 32% are seaweed/macroalgae/CCA, 18% are rubble/rock, and 10% are sand.

articleTitle: Shallow Water Low-Frequency Propagation Loss Predictions and Measurements Towards Acoustic Range Characterization
abstract: Low-frequency ship noise negatively impacts marine ecosystems and interferes with marine mammal communications. In an effort to manage and reduce ship noise in marine environments, high-fidelity propagation loss measurements were conducted across multiple locations to develop a principled shallow water ranging methodology that improves the accuracy of shallow water ship ranging. This paper reports on a proposed propagation loss procedure and presents preliminary results from in-water tests. Calibrated acoustic projectors, driven by a programmable function generator, were used to simulate different types of ship noise. A surface-mounted, near-field hydrophone, and a pair of bottom-mounted, far-field hydrophones were used to receive the acoustic signals. Propagation loss (PL) was estimated from the near-field and far-field hydrophones to yield source level (SL) estimates. These SL estimates were compared with the calibrated acoustic projector's known source levels to verify the propagation loss accuracy. Future work will further develop PL estimation, resulting in a shallow water ranging technique with a performance comparable to that of deep water ranging.

articleTitle: A New Design of a Portable, Passive Acoustic Buoy for Real-Time Detection of Vocal Marine Mammals
abstract: This paper describes the design, build and operation of portable, passive acoustic buoys (P-PAB) with soft tethered hydrophones, capable of real-time satellite signal transmission to shore. We describe the set of commercial components used in the system, reliability of communications, power usage, duty cycle, as well as the at-sea deployment logistics.

articleTitle: Modelling of ROV-Operated Disconnectable Mooring Systems in Wave Dominated Environments
abstract: Floating offshore wind turbines (FOWTs) hold immense potential for unlocking previously inaccessible offshore wind resources, with recent advancements positioning the technology on the brink of commercial success. Central to the success of FOWT projects is the optimization of operations and maintenance (O&M) procedures, particularly concerning mooring system design and the utilization of Remotely Operated Vehicles (ROVs), This paper presents an analysis of mooring line disconnection activities using state-of-the-art ROV technology, focusing on the impact of mooring connector depth with the Arven Offshore Wind Farm serving as a case study. Utilizing a simplified two degree of freedom dynamic ROV model and hindcast metocean data, the study examines the station-keeping ability of an ROV subject to wave perturbations, evaluating the effect of depth on mooring connector operational availability. Results indicate that deeper mooring connector installations substantially enhance mooring connector availability from less than 10 % at 5 m depth to over 90 % at 20 m depth, thereby reducing weather-related delays and improving operational efficiency. Furthermore, a sensitivity analysis on ROV power highlights potential avenues for enhancing accessibility without necessitating mooring design modifications. These findings underscore the importance of integrating FOWT O&M strategies and installation considerations with mooring design at an early stage by accounting for realistic performance of ROV-operated tasks, ultimately contributing to the competitiveness and success in the offshore wind sector.

articleTitle: Using the Model for Ambient Sound Levels Underwater from Wind (MUSLAW) to Estimate Wind Speeds
abstract: A model that generates a time series of underwater sound from the wind has recently been proposed. The model incorporates water and receiver depths, sound speed profile, bottom sediment type, and the wind speed. Here the modelled sound levels are compared with measured sound levels collected over two years at six locations as part of the Atlantic Deepwater Ecosystem Observatory Network (ADEON) project in the U.S. Mid- and South Atlantic Outer Continental Shelf. The estimated wind speed closely (aligned with)the wind speed from the ERA5 global reanalysis dataset (resolution of ERA5) with an average standard deviation of 1.35. From this comparison, it is concluded that the model provides an accurate representation of the underwater sound from wind. The model may be used to estimate wind speed, when given sediment type and when the acoustic data are well calibrated, have few artefacts in the frequency range of 1– 15 kHz, and there are a few other sound sources present besides wind.

articleTitle: Powering Oceans 3.0: the Low Latency Computing Environment Developed by Ocean Networks Canada
abstract: Ocean Networks Canada (ONC) operates a comprehensive suite of ocean observatories that continuously stream vast quantities of oceanographic, physical, and biochemical data. A critical component of this system is the need for low-latency computing, particularly when using MATLAB for processing. Traditional approaches proved inadequate for the required low-latency applications. To address this, ONC introduced “MATLAB-as-a-service,” an in-house solution to eliminate MATLAB startup latency by maintaining a pool of running MATLAB instances. MATLAB-as-a-service integrates with ONC's Oceans 3.0, significantly enhancing the responsiveness of data processing tasks, such as automated testing, which is now completed in three hours instead of eight. This paper outlines the key architecture, components, and operational benefits of MATLAB-as-a-service, demonstrating its effectiveness in overcoming latency challenges when using MATLAB for processing.

articleTitle: Navigation for Multiple Short Term ADCP Measurements Using an Autonomous Underwater Landing Vehicle (AULV)
abstract: Recent increases in research and development of the marine energy sector requires an in-depth knowledge of marine currents. This is obtained with current profilers. The Autonomous Underwater Landing Vehicle (AULV) is designed for the deployment of a current profiler with minimal human intervention. The AULV allows for accurate positioning of the Acoustic Doppler Current Profiler (ADCP), and reduced safety risks associated with manual labor or diver involvement for deploying an ADCP, as it can dive and resurface autonomously, and transmit collected data wirelessly. The vehicle has a positioning accuracy of the vehicle is within a 1-meter radius, can dive at a depth of up to 10 meters, and be operated for up to 150 hours.

articleTitle: Performance of Underwater Optical Communication with Solar Interference Mitigation
abstract: Underwater optical wireless communication has risen as a promising technology to realize high-rate links supporting many different activities and applications. Differently from acoustic communication representing the most effective transmission method in underwater environment, optical signaling suffers from the effect of sunlight, acting as interference and potentially degrading the link performance. In this regard, our paper investigates the reliability of an underwater optical communication in presence of solar interference. Specifically, we propose a novel mechanism for joint channel and solar interference estimation, driving signal detection at the receiver. Performance are evaluated for different modulation schemes, and the results demonstrate the importance of an accurate sunlight interference estimation and rejection in order to achieve good robustness to detection errors.

articleTitle: SimpleModem: A Low Cost Acoustic Modem Implementation for In-Situ Sensing Applications
abstract: SimpleModem is a simple, low-cost, modular modem architecture designed for use with many different acoustic actuators for the marine sensing research and hobbyist communities. Dense in-situ sensing networks require large numbers of low-cost communication systems that integrate seamlessly with arbitrary sensor, actuation and power systems. SimpleModem's easy-to-learn architecture will enable future development of a wide variety of such sensor systems. SimpleModem implements a 430/360 Hz frequency-shift keying (FSK) Protocol, encoded via a simple assembly language routine and decoded using an array of operational amplifiers; a complete explanation of firmware and signals analysis is included herein. Schematics for the full system, along with the simple low-level programs are provided. The SimpleModem architecture is designed to work with future interchangeable acoustic actuators, enabling communication through water, air and high density sediments.

articleTitle: Trajectory Tracking of Underactuated Marine Vessels with Inputs Saturations
abstract: This paper considers the trajectory tracking prob-lem for a class of underactuated marine vessels in the presence of inputs saturations. Indeed, this physical input saturation is a very common phenomenon in various practical applications, often causing a degradation in system performance and potentially leading to system instability. In addition to present a novel scheme for trajectory tracking of underactuated system, in this paper we apply a sort of auxiliary or augmented system concept to deal with this input saturations. This concept is not new in this paper, however, through detailed investigation of its design procedure, we find out that it is possible for us to (significantly) improve the tracking performance through proper design of the control parameters. Numerical study is also carried out to verify the effectiveness of the proposed tracking scheme.

articleTitle: Unplugged with ONC's Super Pump: A Reversing Pump that Mitigates CTD Data Loss Due to Sediment Blockage
abstract: Ocean Networks Canada, an initiative of the University of Victoria, operates cabled ocean observatories that allow for collection of near real-time, high-frequency water property observations via CTD (Conductivity, Temperature, Depth) and dissolved oxygen (DO) instruments. Continuous, long-term time series from these instruments are needed for establishing environmental baselines, studying physical ocean dynamics, and detecting regional change. In recent years, the CTD/DOs deployed in coastal, near-bottom, sediment and particle laden environments have been fraught with severe data quality issues caused by material load into the instruments' internal plumbing. Here we present a mechanical solution, the Super Pump, that capitalizes on ONC network's near unrestricted power to circulate a heavy flow of water through the CTD/DO plumbing, on-demand. Two successful deployments of the Super Pump at coastal observatories suggest the pump substantially reduces data loss.

articleTitle: Combining Low Cost Imaging and Fluorescence Spectroscopy to Assess a Nile Red Counterstain for Differentiating Microplastic and Organic Particles
abstract: Microplastics (MPs) are small fragments of plastic debris that have become pervasive in the natural environment due to their lightweight, durable nature and diminutive size. The fluorescent dye Nile Red has become increasingly popular for staining and detecting microplastics using the naked eye or visual imaging. However, microplastic detection using Nile Red alone is susceptible to false positives caused by stained or autofluorescent organic materials. Counterstaining, which introduces a fluorescent stain that binds preferentially to organic materials, is an emerging method to reduce false positives when tagging plastics with Nile Red. However, few studies characterize the fluorescence emission spectra of particles stained with Nile Red and a counterstain. To assess the viability of a counterstain for altering the spectra of organic materials that may otherwise be mistaken for plastics, fluorescence spectra were gathered for organic materials stained with Nile Red and a counterstain Calcofluor White and Evans Blue for the first time. The particles were then imaged alongside plastics stained with a mixture of Nile Red and the counterstain to ascertain if organic materials could be visually differentiated based on the counterstain. The presented methods contribute to developing accessible microplas-tic detection technologies,

articleTitle: Virtual Tethered Autonomous Underwater Vehicle Using Multimodal Communications
abstract: The collection of seafloor data, especially high-resolution images and video, can help researchers better understand the sea environment. Considering mobility, autonomous underwater vehicles (AUVs) are widely used to carry various data collection tools for seafloor data collection. Data collected by the AUV is challenging to retrieve in real time due to limitations in underwater communications. We propose the use of multimodal communications incorporating both acoustic and optical to allow the AUV to be virtually tethered to the surface vehicle during underwater surveys. Based on the path of the surface vehicle, the AUV carries out underwater data collection and then real-time data upload. We trained the reinforcement learning policy to control the AUV tracking the surface vehicle during underwater surveys, maintaining virtual tethers through multimodal communications. The trained policy is tested in the simulated environment and will be deployed on actual machines in the future.

articleTitle: Software Integration and Interoperability: Upgrading ROV Jason's Motor Control Propulsion System
abstract: This paper presents the integration of ELMO (Elmo Motion Controls) motor controllers into the National Deep Submergence Facility's control system for the ROV Jason. The upgraded topside software maintains compatibility with legacy MTS (MTS Systems Corporation) motor controllers while enhancing thruster performance and monitoring. Key improvements include a motor control driver design without relying on state machine patterns, robust fault detection, and failsafe mechanisms. The system's GUI was enhanced for seamless control of both new and legacy thrusters. Custom electronics were added to monitor controller pod status and environmental parameters. Extensive testing validated the system's functionality under real-world conditions. This upgrade significantly advances ROV technology, enhancing system reliability, monitoring capabilities, and overall performance for deep-sea scientific missions.

articleTitle: A Clustering-Aided Template Matching Algorithm Towards Underwater SLAM Using Imaging Sonar
abstract: In man-made marine infrastructures, elements such as pillars, cables or ducts are common, which provide distinctive landmarks for Simultaneous Localization and Mapping purposes. In this work, we concentrate on the application of template matching to acoustic imagery for landmark detection and tracking, building on the modeling of common elements in marine environments. The proposed algorithm extends on the original method by employing a density-based clustering technique for match candidate selection and leveraging vehicle inertial information to identify regions of interest in the acquired images, tackling performance deterioration resulting from motion-induced image deformation and overall acoustic feature ambiguity. Experimental results are provided based on datasets collected in a testing pool environment.

articleTitle: AI-Quifer - Using Artificial Intelligence to Determine Offshore Groundwater Occurrences That are Key to Coastal Water Management
abstract: The current stress on global freshwater supply highlights the importance to further investigate the presence of offshore freshened groundwater (OFG), a resource that is estimated to amount to 10 to 100 times the global volume of freshwater consumed over the last 100 years. In line with recent developments in terrestrial data-driven groundwater modelling, we propose that globally available geospatial data (e.g. Digital Elevation Models, global groundwater models, geological and seafloor information), in conjunction with climatic data, can be used to predict the largely hidden offshore occurrence of coastal freshwater aquifers. Specifically, we aim to derive a reliable machine learning method that will account for the complex underlying hydrological mechanism of offshore groundwater emplacement and preservation. Here we present the results of the first phase of the AI-quifer project; (1) the derivation of proxi attributes (indicators) that are representative of the hydrogeological processes controlling OFG, and (2) the preparation of geological cross sections (orthogonally to the coastline) to augment the ML training data and evaluate the behaviour and influence of hydraulic conditions on the development of OFG due to changing boundary conditions (transmission from glacial to interglacial or vice versa).

articleTitle: Challenges and Opportunities of Standards for AI Methods for Ocean Applications
abstract: AI methods have established their role in different domains and is becoming pervasive also in environmental sciences like meteorology. Excellent examples of the efficiency of AI methods can be found in applications like pattern recognition in images or the analysis acoustic data. The advantage is that a large amount of data can be checked automatically and without human intervention. The situation is different with time series data, where the amount of data is not very large, and the interpretation must be combined with physical or biochemical models. What is still seen as an obstacle to a more thorough use of AI methods, especially machine learning, is the fact that ML algorithms are purely data-driven and only take modeling into account to a limited extent and are therefore not directly suitable for a validation system. Besides the selection of the right model for the individual science case there is also the issue of validating the resulting data and information. The role of standards in this context needs to be discussed and defined in order to pave the way for a wider adoption of AI methods.

articleTitle: 3D Dubins Paths for Underwater Vehicles
abstract: The dynamics of unmanned underwater vehicles (UUVs) impose significant constraints on the types of paths that can be followed. A number of motion models have been proposed that are inspired by the Dubins vehicle model. We have investigated two state-of-the-art models that ensure a bounded turning rate, bounded pitch angle, and (in one case) a bounded pitch change rate. We will show that these existing models can produce undesirable solutions (or even no solutions) between an initial and final pose of a UUV. Here, we present a new model that combines these two models, preserves the best features of both, and is empirically shown to connect any arbitrary start and goal pose. We also present results that show how the new model can be used as a local planner in sampling-based algorithms.
