articleTitle: Innovative Hydrophone Arrays for Sound Mapping in Underwater Environments
abstract: Sound mapping is a technique to visualize sound using acoustic arrays which could enhance traditional inspection of subsea equipment. The Smart Underwater Sound Imager (SUSI) is a portable planar hydrophone array that offers high-resolution sound mapping, making it a specialized tool for this purpose. By mapping sound, we gain a new perspective on the noise produced by underwater equipment, opening new possibilities for understanding and mitigating its impact. This paper describes the array technology and presents results from field tests and a baseline inspection.

articleTitle: Low Cost Wave Maker for Educational Applications
abstract: Environmental education is steadily becoming a more prominent and vital area of learning, specifically because of the ever-changing conditions found on Earth. Making this education accessible to students is vital in promoting positive change and environmental awareness. A major aspect of education is designing interactive as well as innovative methods of engagement for students. Hands-on activities that involve real world practice or models are extremely effective. In the realm of environmental science, activities such as these would greatly help students develop green skills, adapt to the harsh reality of a warming world, and understand how to better combat climate change [1]. One of the specific categories in which this evolving topic is extremely relevant is in the study of the Earth's oceans. Organizations such as MIT Sea Grant are pushing the boundaries of ocean engineering and part of this mission involves the development of tools and resources to further education for collegiate, high school, and middle school students. One of these cutting-edge tools is a wave-generator. In January of 2024 a team of MIT Students and faculty began designing and creating a series of wave generator designs that could be easily implemented in the classroom setting. This entailed designing a mechanism that was both portable and easy to assemble allowing for scholastic use as well as the eventual up-scaling to larger testing environments. This wave maker can assist teachers and professors around the globe in generating comprehensive lesson plans that are adaptive, teaching students about different ways to account for as well as handle the constantly fluctuating environments of the ocean. Although there are some pre-existing models for wave making machines, this educational wave maker that we have designed provides a cost effective, convenient, and simple method of generating waves with specific dimensions, speeds, and frequencies, given that it consists of a scotch yoke linkage system that makes use of a plunging wedge [2]. This whole assembly is mounted on a portable frame that can be attached to different sized tanks. The arms of the linkage system themselves are adjustable to enable different plunge depths, along with the size of the wedge and the speed at which the wedge is plunged into the water. This multidimensional adjustability combined with the research done on the generation of specific wave types allows for a consistent and stable method of generating a unique wave for any given lesson plan. The parts used to construct the wave maker are all extremely cost-effective and can be easily obtained by scholastic STEM programs. The other parts used in the wave-maker's design are quick and easy to fabricate and can be easily pre-made if a school does not have access to the necessary tools. After testing the educational wave maker we found that by controlling the speed and stroke of the plunging system we can accurately change the dimensions of our waves. We also observed that the mechanism itself is both durable and easily portable, a vital part of bringing our goal of accessibility to life. At Sea Grant we will continue to develop the mechanism and find ways to effectively improve its function.

articleTitle: A Project Development Perspective of the Reoxygenation of Marine Dead Zones
abstract: Marine dead zones are an increasing problem worldwide.

articleTitle: Automation of Environmental Data Collection Through the Commercial Fishing Industries
abstract: This report provides an overview of the environmental data collection platform paired with the unique opportunities that Rope on Command (ROC) fishing has created. We will show how the data is stored on the device, collected passively from the end user's system, and stored securely for data aggregation and data analysis opportunities.

articleTitle: Characterization of Onboard Wind by Comparing Two Anemometers
abstract: Characteristics of onboard wind measurements and hull effects were investigated by comparing the onboard wind on starboard and port sides of a ship. The wind directions and speeds measured by both anemometers were roughly in agreement on average. However, deviation often exceeded the of Ficial accuracy, and the trend on wind direction differed depending on the wind direction. The wind direction gap is large on the wind direction where only one anemometer is influenced by the structures. The wind direction gap is small on the wind direction where is no structures. The winds from −100~+ 100 are influenced by the main mast, and go around the aft side of the main mast. Wind from aft side is more likely to blow through on lee-side. Wind from fore-side is intercepted and reduced. The winds from between the bow <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim\pm 100^{\circ}$</tex> are influenced by the main mast, and go around aft side of the main mast. The winds from between stern <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\sim\pm 110^{\circ}$</tex> are influenced by the aft structures, and go around fore side of the structures. Wind from <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$\pm 80^{\circ}\sim\pm 140^{\circ}$</tex> is more likely to blow through, so the wind speed is larger on the lee-side. The wind from the directions which are intercepted by the main must and the aft structures is reduced on the lee-side.

articleTitle: FNO Tsunami Flooding Simulation for Arbitrary Bathymetries, Shorelines, and Land Topographies
abstract: Global warming is rapidly melting glaciers, causing sea levels to rise and shorelines to encroach on communities and animal habitats. This results in coastal erosion, increased storm surges, and habitat loss, such as the breeding grounds of elephant seals. More critically, higher sea levels heighten community vulnerability to tsunamis, which can generate massive waves that overwhelm sea walls, as evidenced in Indonesia and Japan. Thus, simulating tsunami flooding is crucial. While SWASH, a tool based on shallow water equations, effectively models complex environments like ports and residential areas, it is slow, taking 4 hours on 16 CPU cores for one simulation. In contrast, we have developed neural operators that significantly speed up this process. Our neural operators, trained on hundreds of input-output image pairs, convert a 2.5D input image of the simulation environment into an output image showing the predicted flooding state, including wave height and wet-and-dry states. Benchmark tests show our neural operators complete simulations in just 1.2 seconds, compared to 7 hours for traditional finite volume solvers. This speed advantage remains regardless of input grid dimensions. While our neural operators excel at predicting the wet or dry state, further training is needed to improve wave height predictions. Figures demonstrate our neural operators' ability to predict flooding at various times given a simulation environment input. Our methodology offers a faster, efficient alternative for tsunami flooding simulations, which is crucial for enhanced disaster preparedness.

articleTitle: Remote Piloting Development of an ROV
abstract: This work presents a project that consists of turning a commercial Remote Operated Vehicle (ROV) into a Remotely Piloted ROV. It was taken two approaches. First we developed a serial/ethernet converter to transfer data from the hand controller to the ROV control console and vice-versa. In this approach, an ESP32 microcontroller was used to receive serial data in the 9-bit framing protocol and transmit them over a network connection. The reverse operation was carried out on the other side by another ESP32. The second approach was based on replacing the ROV remote control with an Single Board Computer (SBC), whose function was to emulate the signals sent to the ROV by the remote control. It will be presented the development and the achieved results for these two methods.

articleTitle: Leg-Pattern Modeling for Swimming of Underwater Walking Robot Considering Hydrodynamic Forces
abstract: The needs for underwater robots increased to explore and develop ocean resources safely and efficiently. Traditionally propeller-based ROVs(Remotely Operated Vehicles) and AUVs(Autonomous Unmanned Vehicles) have been used for ocean exploration and development. However, over the past decade, a new type of underwater robot that uses legs has emerged. These robots offer advantages such as stable movement over uneven or complex sea floor terrains and minimizing ecosystem disruption. However, due to legged locomotion, they have slower movement speeds compared to traditional underwater robots. To overcome this limitation, a swimming function using legs has been introduced. This paper aims to discuss the design of the swimming motion for underwater legged robots. Additionally, we define the hydrodynamic resistance that occurs due to swimming with legs underwater and calculate it to determine the thrust generated during swimming.

articleTitle: What is the Maximum Power Output of NEPTUNE?
abstract: The NEPTUNE cabled observatory commenced operations in 2009 as the world's first regional-scale seafloor infrastructure providing long-term continuous power and data connectivity for ocean instrumentation. The observatory's power system was designed for resiliency to faults and with sufficient capacity to allow expansion to new locations with higher power loads. In its lifetime there has been a steady increase in quantities of oceanographic instrumentation, but these devices are typically designed to consume minimal power. The impacts of a concentrated power load are not well understood because the observatory has historically only used small fraction of available power, and because the network is not a trivial linear DC circuit. The Pacific Ocean Neutrino Experiment project (P-ONE) proposes adding a neutrino detector to the observatory which will create substantial power demands at one instrumented site. This paper investigates the theoretical power limit for P-ONE and the stability impact on NEPTUNE by exploring systemic failure mechanisms.

articleTitle: Noise Source Direction of Arrival Estimation in the New England Mud Patch Using Acoustic Vector Sensors
abstract: The Seabed Characterization Experiment 2022 (SBCEXP 2022) was conducted in the New England Mud Patch (NEMP) and shelf break areas from May 6, 2022 to June 6, 2022. The experiment aimed to collect active and passive acoustic data supporting the development and comparison between geoacoustic inversion data sets. Various acoustic sensors were deployed to collect this data, including Vertical Line Arrays (VLA) and Ocean Bottom Recorders (OBX). Additional contextual data, such as Automatic Identification System (AIS) ship tracking data showing vessel traffic in the experiment area, was also collected. The measurements presented in this paper utilize data collected from OBXs and the logged AIS data to estimate the direction of arrival (DOA) of ship noise and active acoustic sources using only passive acoustic data. The OBX sensors deployed in the experiment are acoustic vector sensors capable of capturing sound pressure and particle velocity measurements in all three dimensions. This dimensional information can be leveraged to generate DOA estimations using beamforming techniques. Multiple DOA estimation algorithms, including the Multiple Signal Classification (MUSIC) method and the Capon method (also known as minimum-variance distortionless beamforming), are used to analyze OBX data and make DOA estimates for noise sources. These estimates are then compared to processed AIS data, showing ship position and track in the NEMP. Underwater noise pollution from shipping traffic is pervasive globally [1]. DOA data from ship noise sources on the ocean surface can provide contextual information for maritime surveillance and security, environmental monitoring, ship navigation and traffic management, scientific research, and search and rescue operations. The data processed and presented in this paper show the detection and azimuth tracking of vessels in the shipping lane and the active sources deployed for SBCEXP 2022. The results demonstrate the possibility of monitoring underwater noise pollution sources using a single acoustic vector sensor. The successful application of the DOA estimation techniques with acoustic vector sensors underscores their utility in passive acoustic monitoring by providing DOA data essential for operational and environmental noise mitigation and monitoring strategies in heavily trafficked marine areas. The advantages of using a single sensor package are that it allows noise sources to be monitored with relative ease of deployment and low cost. Additional sensors can be deployed to enhance detection capabilities and provide more accurate noise source localization. This paper compares different DOA estimation techniques and scenarios where they can be applied.

articleTitle: Earthquake and Seaquake Analysis for a 15MW Semi-Submersible Floating Offshore Wind Turbine (FOWT)
abstract: It is important to investigate the possible impact of earthquakes on Floating offshore Wind Turbines (FOWTs) to be installed near volcanic zone, such as Ring of Fire in California. In this study, we propose a procedure for numerical implementation of earthquake and seaquake loads on FOWTs. Seaquake potential satisfying 3D Helmholtz equation is calculated by hybrid integral equation method. The pre-calculated seaquake load time-series is inputted to fully coupled aero-servo-hydro-mooring-dynamic analysis program. A three-column 15MW semi-submersible FOWT is used with El Centro past earthquake record scaled based on the spectral matching method targeting one offloating wind farm leasing areas (Morro Bay, California). Numerical analysis shows that incorporation of seaquake load is insignificant in platform motion and mooring tensions responses, but nacelle z-acceleration can be appreciably increased due to high frequency content of earthquakes and seaquake loads.

articleTitle: Evaluation of the Environmental Impacts Due to Floating Offshore Wind Farms
abstract: Around the world, the utilization of technologies powered by so-called renewable energy sources is in progressive development, and this is a major factor in the move toward a cleaner and more efficient energy system. The move toward more sustainable alternative energy sources enables the possibility of producing electricity without emitting greenhouse gases, thanks to the reduced use of fossil. Wind and solar power are major players in the current energy transition. The limits of land availability for wind farm installation have led in recent times to focus more research on the study of different types of wind turbines for offshore applications. In this regard, the paper presents a case study in Mazara del Vallo (Trapani, Italy) for an offshore wind farm power generation with subsequent estimation of environmental impacts.

articleTitle: The Application of Best Practices for Optimizing Merchant Ship Speed in the Context of Reducing Greenhouse Gas Emissions
abstract: Proud of its maritime traditions, the merchant marine often struggles to adapt to new modes of operation. This dynamic makes the shipping industry a very conservative one. In a rapidly changing world, with the major challenge posed by climate change and the advent of artificial intelligence, ship managers need to be more involved. We should not just wait for technological solutions which will only mature in several years, but rather rethink our ways of doing things to be more efficient. With this in mind, this article presents concrete measures which can be implemented immediately to optimize shipping, thereby reducing GHG emissions while generating financial gains.

articleTitle: Improved Three-Dimensional Terrain-Aided AUV Navigation Using Error State Filtering
abstract: Kalman filtering has been commonly used in terrain-aided navigation (TAN) applications for autonomous underwater vehicles (AUVs) where digital terrain maps are available and bottom terrains are sufficiently varied. Current Kalman filtering based TAN literature notably lacks an explicit consideration of navigational sensor bias errors which can have impacts on positioning accuracy and payload sensor data such as sonars. This paper builds on our previous work on 2D TAN by investigating the performance of a low-cost AUV navigating underwater in 3D and estimating navigational sensor bias errors using existing digital terrain maps using an error-state, extended Kalman filter (ES-EKF). Preliminary results based on Monte-Carlo runs suggest that ES-EKF can effectively estimate the vehicle position (Initial error < 132 m), velocity, orientation, most sensor biases, and small ocean currents (< 0.5 m/s).

articleTitle: A Guided AUV for Underwater Plume Estimation
abstract: A concentration estimator for a contaminant plume generated by an underwater source is presented. The plant includes a stationary or mobile source and the resulting plume. An autonomous underwater vehicle (AUV) is equipped with sensors and uses a process-state hybrid estimator to make real-time predictions of the plume. The plume is modeled by the 3D advection-diffusion equation. The underwater source follows a physics-based prescribed trajectory. The AUV is modeled using a 6 DOF dynamical model for underwater vehicles and is guided by a PID controller. The estimator is discretized using a Non Overlapping Domain Decomposition Explicit Finite Volume Method (NODDE-FVM) with constant time 4th order Runge-Kutta integration. Numerical results for the plant and estimator are presented for a case of a continuous release from a moving source in realistic ambient conditions. The effectiveness of the guidance model and controller for the AUV is assessed.

articleTitle: Enhancing Fisheries Management in with OLSPS Commercial Fishing Electronic Logbook Solutions Amos Barkai OLSPS
abstract: Most of the world's commercial fish stocks are heavily depleted and an estimated 70\% of fish populations are biologically and economically vulnerable and depleted to well below their Maximum Sustainable Yield (MSY) due to sustained overfishing. In addition, large proportion of the commercial fisheries are mixed species fishing operations. These fisheries tend to target a few economically important species. However, due to the indiscriminate nature of many fishing methods there is a wide variety of bycatch species that are captured and either discarded or landed. In some fisheries there is a limit on the amount of bycatch that can be landed (chock species) and once this limit is reached fishing must stop altogether even if the legal quota of the target species wasn't yet reached. Bycatch of commercial fisheries worldwide is of great concern to fisheries’ managers, scientists, and environmental and conservation groups. Bycatch contributes to changing the structure of marine communities and ecosystems, leading to significant implications for marine populations and the overall health and sustainability of the marine ecosystems. As a result, the total impact of fishing on marine ecosystems may far exceed what can be estimated and assumed by only looking and monitoring the landed catch of commercial species. One should add to this, documented cases where other marine life are killed and sensitive ecosystems are destroyed due to rampant fishing even (maybe mainly) by legally operating fishing vessels and the public and scientific concerns regarding the adverse impact of commercial fishing on the marine ecosystem as whole is probably well founded.

articleTitle: A Marine Autonomous Systems Digital Twin; Bringing Value to Researchers, Data Users and Vehicle Operations
abstract: The upscaling of the use of autonomous ocean observing platforms in line with Whitt et al. (2020) has created the requirements for improved interfaces to enable efficient and interactive piloting of marine autonomous platforms. Such interfaces will enable scalable operations that make use of pilots who are accountable for the operation of platforms, enabling more interactive control of the platforms to facilitate researchers to be closer to vehicle operations, and maximize the value of observations for different user types e.g. synoptic surveys for blue skies research versus the needs of operational ocean models Independently of the evolution in autonomous ocean platforms, the concept of digital twins has emerged and has attained prominence within ocean oceanography by activities like the UN Decade for sustainable ocean development digital twin of the ocean programme. Thus, digital twins have the potential to facilitate efficient and interactive operations of platforms with a low technical barrier for users, and be interoperable with related tools such as digital twins for decision making by policy makers. These developments and concepts are being brought together in the Marine Autonomous Systems Digital Twin (MAS-DT) project with three goals: 1. Enable researcher to have more control of ocean glider operations on projects while retaining pilot accountability. 2. Increase the value of ocean glider observations to operational ocean models. 3. Make the operation of increasingly complex ocean glider missions more efficient for autonomous vehicle pilots MAS-DT will bring together visualization of operations, AI to aid decision making and develop a work flow that meets the needs of researcher and platform pilots. MAS-DT will develop the digital twin within the NOC Command and Control systems (C2) for autonomous platforms incorporating new AI based decision making tools developed by the Oxford Robotics Institute. This paper will present the design of MAS-DT prior to formal trials on exemplar glider deployments later in 2024.

articleTitle: Neural Operator Simulation of Turbulent Multiphase Flow with Applications in Ocean Wave Modeling
abstract: Global warming has increased ocean wave heights and the frequency of extreme wave events. As a result, ocean waves have contributed to more coastal erosion, flooding, and fatigue damage of ocean-based structures. Researchers interested in understanding the effects of ocean waves must rely on slow numerical methods such as particle-in-cell (PIC), which can take hours. Therefore, researchers have good occasion to find a faster alternative for modeling ocean waves. Here, we present a Fourier Neural Operator (FNO) for predicting ocean wave behavior on grids of arbitrary geometry. An FNO is designed to map an input image to an output image in infinite dimensions. This allows the FNO to act as a solution operator, which decreases computational complexity. To create data for our FNO, we used the PIC method to create 290 simulations of an ocean wave crashing against a random obstruction, i.e., some arbitrary geometry. Each simulation modeled 38,000 water particles for 600 time steps, which required 30 minutes. From these simulations, we created training and testing datasets of 274 and 16 image pairs, respectively. We trained the FNO for 75 epochs, which took 900 seconds. After training, we validated the FNO against our 16 test points. At a resolution of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$256 \times 256$</tex>, our FNO had an inference time of only 0.073 second. Our FNO results were good, especially since only 274 training points were used. Using our approach, FNOs can be designed to predict levee overtopping, flooding, blast waves, and the effect of water drops over wildfires.

articleTitle: Iceberg Profiling Autonomy Using Elliptical Trajectories
abstract: In this work, autonomy is developed for an uncrewed underwater vehicle (UUV) equipped with a multi-beam sonar to perform precise profiling maneuvers to map underwater iceberg topography using a novel method involving elliptical trajectories. Given a general estimate of the profile, elliptical survey swathes are generated at various depths based on vehicle, sensor, and mission constraints, and these trajectories are implemented in an iceberg-centric coordinate frame to incorporate iceberg drift and rotational motion. Finally, autonomy and guidance methods are developed and implemented for the vehicle to track these trajectories and complete the profiling mission. The developed system is tested in a simulation environment using 4-degree of freedom dynamics for a variety of realistic iceberg profiles using point-cloud representations to validate performance, practicality, and robustness.

articleTitle: Aeon for Ocean: Educating Kids About Oceans in Their Habitat
abstract: Marine animals capture the imagination of all children. Kids who live in coastal areas have the opportunity to observe the ocean habitat firsthand. But children who live inland in landlocked states often do not benefit from that connection and are less likely to become interested in ocean life and marine conservation. In this paper, we focus on how we can educate these children about oceans and marine life to promote awareness about the ocean and our impact on it, which leads to more actions to protect it, and the outcomes of these methods. Our methods include presentations, virtual reality experiences, hands-on projects, online lessons, interviews with industry experts, and the Teacher Ambassador program, which provides teachers with opportunities to educate and empower youth within their learning community. Through data from schools and our social media platforms, we demonstrated the effectiveness of these approaches in educating the landlocked community about oceans, marine life, the impact we have on the ocean and vice versa.

articleTitle: A Fast and Precise Digital Lock-In Amplifier for Accessible in-situ Fluorometry
abstract: The in-situ fluorometer is a ubiquitous tool for monitoring marine and freshwater environments, from detection of algal blooms to performing dye-tracing studies for Ocean Alkalinity Enhancement for Marine Carbon Dioxide Removal. Low-cost open-source instrumentation has been identified as a potential solution to both the demand for data and the need for greater accessibility. In this paper, we present a Digital Lock-In Amplifier designed for the Texas Instruments MSP430 platform, in the context of its central role in a new open-source in-situ fluorometer, the PIXIE. The amplifier is implemented digitally, using the mixed signal peripherals of the TI MSP430FG6626 microcontroller to minimize PCB complexity. DSP is performed using a Lattice Wave Digital Filter and a Q3.28 fixed-point arithmetic designed to maximize use of the MSP430's hardware multiplier for speed, precision, and numerical stability. The design and implementation of the lock-in amplifier, along with its performance metrics and example data collected by the PIXIE, are provided.

articleTitle: An ICI Canceling Underwater OFDM Communication System with 2-Step Modified Delay and Doppler Profiler
abstract: In 2023, the first prototype of an Inter-Carrier-Interference (ICI) Canceling Underwater Orthogonal Frequency Division Multiplexing (OFDM) Communication system was proposed using modified Delay and Doppler Profiler (mDDP). However, the Bit Error Rate (BER) reduction was limited. As a result of continuous research, we found that the two-stage configuration of mDDP can dramatically improve BER reduction performance. This paper presents the results of pool experiments of OFDM communications in forward and reverse two-wave Doppler-shift environments. To mitigate the ICI effect, a modified Delay and Doppler Profiler (mDDP), which estimates not only attenuation, relative delay and Doppler shift but also sampling clock shift of each multi-path component, is utilized. After the 1st stage mDDP, the effect of ICI has been reduced from the Channel Transfer Function (CTF) and the more accurate CTF is processed by the second-stage mDDP, resulting in highly accurate channel parameter estimation and improved ICI cancellation in the final multi-tap equalizer. To verify this effect, two transmit transducers and one receive transducer were used in the pool experiment to create a two-wave inverse Doppler-shifted multipath environment. By increasing the number of equalizer taps, the BER reduction performance of 64QAM modulation was improved by approximately one order of magnitude for 2step mDDP compared to 1step mDDP.

articleTitle: A Hybrid CNN-Transformer Network for Global Ocean Wind Speed Retrieval from GNSS-R Data
abstract: Global navigation satellite system reflectometry (GNSS-R) has emerged as a promising technique for global sea surface wind speed measurement. Currently, a lot of methods based on convolutional neural networks (CNNs) have been developed to extract features from delay Doppler maps (DDMs) and retrieve wind speed from GNSS-R data. However, CNNs emphasize local features and cannot capture global features due to their inherent locality. In order to address this limitation, a hybrid CNN-Transformer Network (CTN) is proposed in this study. Specifically, the hybrid CTN consists of a CNN branch tailored for capturing local features and a Transformer branch for global features. By combining these distinct features, the designed hybrid CTN facilitates a comprehensive representation of DDMs. Experiments conducted on Cyclone GNSS (CYGNSS) data demonstrate improved accuracy and robustness of the proposed method in wind speed retrieval from GNSS-R data.

articleTitle: Bearing Estimation in the Presence of Surface Noise Using a 2D Array
abstract: We consider a rectangular grid of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$m_{\mathrm{h}}$</tex> horizontal by <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$m_{\mathrm{v}}$</tex> vertical hydrophones (in total <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$m=m_{\mathrm{h}}m_{\mathrm{v}}$</tex> elements). The array is mounted on a rigid structure in a plane perpendicular to the sea surface. The array is used to estimate the bearings of sources located in the far field. We analyze the performance gain over a horizontal line array (i.e. an array with <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$m_{\mathrm{v}}=1$</tex> ) where the surface sea noise is the limiting factor. To achieve the directional properties of the noise, a sea surface noise model is proposed. The performance is analyzed for both conventional delay-and-sum (DAS) and Capon (a.k.a minimum variance distortionless response (MVDR)) beamforming. The results show that the output SNR improvement (as a function of <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$m_{\mathrm{v}}$</tex> ) is larger than that achieved with spatially white noise (i.e. noise which is uncorrelated betwen the hydrophones) and that Capon performs better than DAS in the considered scenario. For sample-level simulations, including detection and estimation, the performance of DAS and Capon are similar. A small but significant per-formance advantage of DAS over Capon is observed when the bottom material is highly absorbent and the beamforming is aimed slightly below the target. In that case the downtilt of the DAS beams reduce the impact of the surface noise more than the signal loss is from target off-pointing. However, only a single source is simulated and the improved resolution capabilities of Capon could make it the better solution when several sources are considered.

articleTitle: Consumer-Grade Aerial-Aquatic Speedy Scanner (AASS) for Efficient Underwater Monitoring with Deep Learning
abstract: Traditional marine monitoring techniques, such as line intercept transects, are often inefficient. While contemporary studies utilize autonomous underwater vehicles (AUVs) and the novel Portable Speedy Sea Scanner (P-SSS) to enhance marine monitoring, their widespread adoption is hindered by high costs and labor-intensive operations, with the data quality often failing to justify the investment. This study introduces a novel self-designed amphibious unmanned aerial vehicle (AASS), integrated with deep learning technology, which combines aerial and aquatic imaging capabilities. It surpasses traditional towed underwater survey tools and AUVs in ecological monitoring effectiveness. The research presents the AASS, enhanced with Super-Resolution Reconstruction (SRR) and an improved YOLOv8 detection network. The AASS system significantly improves data acquisition efficiency, capturing high-resolution images that precisely identify and categorize underwater targets. The SRR technique addresses issues like motion blur and low resolution, enhancing the YOLOv8 model's detection accuracy. Notably, the RCAN model achieved the highest mean average precision (mAP) of 78.6% for detecting reconstructed underwater images, with a x4 magnification in image quality showing superior mAP compared to the Bicubic method. These results affirm the efficacy of the proposed method in enhancing underwater ecological monitoring.

articleTitle: Accelerating Operational Oceanography with Uncrewed Systems: Hypoxia Mapping in the Gulf of Mexico
abstract: The Office of Marine and Aviation Operations (OMAO) at NOAA requires the integration of uncrewed technologies to enhance its mission capabilities and understanding of these innovative systems. The University of Southern Mississippi (USM) is leading research to evaluate and compare data collected by several Uncrewed Surface Vehicle (USV) platforms. This study focuses on supporting NOAA's missions to measure hypoxia in the Gulf of Mexico, aiming to provide timely, accurate, and cost-effective information through advanced uncrewed platforms. Our research demonstrates the utility of emerging uncrewed platforms, specifically the Sea Trac Systems SP-48 USV. The study goals were to enhance the operational readiness of these systems and support NOAA's UxS Strategic Plan to integrate uncrewed systems into its operations. Our research focuses on the performance of two USVs during variable sea states, assessing its endurance and accuracy of its hypoxia mapping, particularly in areas historically monitored by crewed data collection missions.

articleTitle: Adaptive Receiver Design for Long-Range Underwater Acoustic Communications
abstract: Long-range data transmission through underwater acoustic (UWA) channel is a challenging issue for underwater acoustic communications (UAC). The issue is reflected in the high path loss to the received signal and non-white background noise. To address this issue, adaptive receiver is designed in this paper. The receiving procedure, including channel estimation and diversity combination can be adaptively tuned to match the channel conditions and background noise. Underwater experiment results demonstrate the effectiveness of the adaptive receiver. Compare with conventional methods, adaptive receiver designed in this paper can achieve about 2 dB improvement for long-range data transmission at a distance of 30 km.

articleTitle: Seafloor Imaging Exploration off the Northeastern Coast of Taiwan Using a Deep-towed Vehicle
abstract: The northeastern part of Taiwan, characterized by volcanic formations from tectonic plate collisions, includes the Datun and Keelung Volcanic Groups and volcanic islands such as Keelung, Huaping, Mienhua, and Pengjia Islets. Recent discoveries of submarine volcanoes off Taiwan's northeastern coast highlight potential for polymetallic hydrothermal sulfide deposits, presenting opportunities for economic and scientific exploration. Utilizing the deep-towed vehicle Abyss Twisted-pair Imaging System (ATIS), seafloor imaging surveys were conducted from 2020 to 2023, covering 25.68 kilometers over 36.24 hours. Key observations include sandy seafloors with hydrothermal activity indicated by abrupt changes in water temperature and gas emissions in the Keelung Islet area; large igneous rocks and hydrothermal activity across eight sites in the Huaping Islet area; and similar large igneous rocks and hydrothermal activity in the Mienhua and Pengjia Islet areas. These findings support ongoing exploration and resource evaluation, providing crucial data for geophysical and geochemical analysis.

articleTitle: Development and Large-Scale Testing of a Low-Cost Acoustic Release System used to Reduce Entanglement Risk in Commercial Trap Fisheries
abstract: Whale, dolphin and turtle entanglements in fishing gear continue to be a problem on a worldwide scale. Conflicts occur most often in areas with high concentrations of marine mammals in waters also having high concentrations of traps, pots, or gillnets. According to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration's (NOAA's) National Report on Large Whale Entanglements Confirmed in the US in 2022, there were 67 confirmed whale entanglements off US coastlines, with the greatest number of cases being found near Cape Cod Massachusetts and Monterey Bay California. In recent years, significant development and testing of new on-demand or rope-less fishing technologies have been reported, including a low cost Timer Release for Rope-less Traps (TR4RT) by Sub Sea Sonics, funded under a NOAA Bycatch Reduction Engineering Program Grant and presented at the 2021 Oceans Conference in San Diego. The TR4RT release was developed as a solution for small scale and inshore fishing boats needing a simple and affordable option for single traps or small trawls in contrast to the complex high-cost acoustic release systems geared toward offshore boats fishing long trawls with a large number of traps. Based on feedback from fishers, we developed an on-demand acoustic version of the same timer system (the Acoustic Release for Rope-less Traps; AR4RT) under support from the NOAA Saltonstall-Kennedy program and Woods Hole Oceanographic Institution. The AR4RT utilizes a motor turn cam release combined with Sub Sea Sonics proven underwater acoustics technology with a 20 year track record. It can be mounted directly on a fishable trap or fitted on a trawl sled. The AR4RT releases system has been successfully used in time area closures on both coasts of the US including in the Southeast (SE) Atlantic Black Sea Bass fishery in a project lead by Sustainable Seas Technology (SST) where the South Atlantic Fishery Management Council is now moving toward making pop-up gear allowable following closure to protect the North Atlantic Right Whale. Recently, a full-scale test was carried out under a California Experimental Fishing Permit for Dungeness Crab, Rock Crab, and Hagfish with 20 fishers purchasing gear to participate. The AR4RT release units were used with Guardian Ropeless Systems (GRS) line handling equipment to remove vertical lines in the water column and allow crab to be harvested for almost 3 additional months after the regular season closed due the presence of whales. Fishers use our Trap Timer gear marking app to display gear locations and transmit corresponding acoustic commands to the underwater releases. We also developed a regulator version of the app and web portal which allows the California Department of Fish and Game and other enforcement agencies to both view and haul subsurface fishing gear. Testing is also being conducted in the New England lobster fishery by the NOAA Northeast Fisheries Science Center and Maine Department of Marine Resources with a handful of fishers using AR4RT and Deepwater AR4RT releases off Maine, Massachusetts, and Rhode Island, and specifically within the South Island Restricted Area. Partnering with both SST and GRS, scaled up outreach, gear refinements (including updates to the DAR4RT) and testing will take place in New England starting in 2024 with support from the National Fish and Wildlife Foundation.

articleTitle: WaveDiff: Underwater Visual Data Enhancement with Wavelet-Accelerated Diffusion
abstract: Unmanned underwater vehicles generally rely on high quality visual data and low latency for the applications of monitoring, exploration and search. Several methods have been proposed to improve underwater visibility by enhancing images taken by cameras using generative methods such as diffusion models. Although diffusion models have proven very useful for visual data enhancement, they enhance images iteratively, making this process computationally inefficient. Current methods primarily focus on improving visibility without addressing operation latency or speed, rendering these methods unsuitable for low bandwidth or fast information tracking. To overcome this, we propose using discrete wavelet transform (DWT) to decompose the image into four frequency components, reducing the spatial dimension. Out of these four components, we use only one as part of the diffusion process. At the end of the diffusion process, we apply the inverse discrete wavelet transform to obtain the enhanced image. This simple strategy helps reduce processing time by 50% with minimal loss in Peak Signal to Noise Ratio (PSNR) and Structure Similarity Index Measure (SSIM) on the LSUI dataset.

articleTitle: Two-Pass Continuous Active Sonar Processing
abstract: Sonar systems using Linear Frequency Modulated (LFM) Continuous Active Sonar (CAS) waveforms can provide a higher target update rate than conventional Pulsed Active Sonar (PAS) waveforms through sub-pulse processing. The higher target update rate promises to improve tracking performance. The drawback of sub-pulse processing is that reducing the duration and bandwidth of the processed waveform decreases the Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR) or Signal-to-Reverberation Ratio (SRR) of the target echoes. Previous work suggests that incoherently averaging CAS sub-pulses can exploit the range-Doppler bias to make an estimate of the target Doppler as well as improve overall detection performance. The drawback of this technique is that the higher target update rate of the CAS waveform is not exploited for tracking. Here a two pass approach is presented that both retains the higher target update rate while simultaneously removing the range-Doppler bias. Results using this two-pass approach will be shown using the Littoral Continuous Active Sonar 2016 sea trial (LCAS16).

articleTitle: Automating Lobster Length Assessments Towards Facilitating Rapid Fisheries-Assisted Sampling
abstract: The sustainable management of fisheries relies heavily on accurate and timely data collection, yet small-scale fisheries often struggle with the limitations of time and resources. This study presents an approach to automating lobster length assessments using a fisheries-assisted sampling technology (FAST) system. The system integrates a fixed-size baseboard, a consumer-grade smartphone or tablet camera, and a Bluetooth-connected scale, enabling rapid and precise data collection. Key-point detection, facilitated by the DeepLabCut framework, and a deterministic algorithm for target region detection are used to accurately measure lobster carapace lengths from digital images. This method significantly reduces manual measurement time and error, allowing for large-scale data collection. The system's effectiveness was validated through field tests, showing high accuracy in identifying key-points on the lobster carapace. This approach not only enhances the efficiency and accuracy of data collection but also has the potential to be adapted for various marine geographical regions, contributing to better-informed fisheries management decisions. Future work will focus on integrating the system into broader fisheries data collection frameworks.

articleTitle: Optimizing an Ocean Current Energy Conversion Device for Powering Marine Sensors
abstract: Ocean sensors are critical for monitoring marine conditions and understanding ocean ecosystems. However, the deployment duration of these sensors is presently limited by their battery lives, resulting in costly and time-consuming maintenance. Previously, the Water and Energy Research Laboratory (WERL), with input from the Commonwealth Scientific and Industrial Research Organisation (CSIRO), sought to overcome this limitation by harvesting energy from ocean currents to power these sensors. They developed an ocean current energy conversion (CEC) device and tested a prototype in a tow tank, the results of which demonstrated the ability to generate at least 1 W of power from currents as slow as 0.27 m/s. These results strongly indicated feasibility of the concept and the value of continued development. Major present goals include reducing its minimum water speed to 0.2 m/s and performing in-ocean testing. The target of 0.2 m/s was identified in the initial feasibility study for the concept and would significantly increase the range of locations in which the CEC device could be deployed. To move towards this slower water speed, WERL is optimizing the device's turbine using computational fluid dynamics (CFD) and CSIRO is improving the device's alternator, electronics, and subsystem integration. For turbine optimization, we used CFD simulations in multiple design-of-experiment studies to identify key turbine blade geometry parameters that influence turbine output at different operating points. This work was used to generate optimized blades, which we manufactured and installed on the CEC device prototype for retesting in the tow tank. The test results showed that we achieved our target minimum water speed of 0.2 m/s. We also developed and validated a predictive mathematical model of the alternator. This, together with a previously-developed predictive model of the overall device, allowed us to study how alternator design parameters affect the device efficiency. We found that a new alternator could improve the device efficiency by 15–20 percentage points compared to the first prototype. We plan to implement improved blades, alternator, and onboard electronics on a new CEC device prototype. This new prototype will then undergo in-ocean testing to demonstrate full field functionality of the concept.

articleTitle: Fault-tolerant SCADA for UAVs In Inaccessible Environments
abstract: Remote locations including but not limited to, far-reaching offshore airspaces, provide limited communications capabilities between equipment and ground stations. The case for DAVs is no exception, all the while requiring swift decisions because of the high speeds, lack of detailed real-time weather data, and complex applications. With the limitations and require-ments at hand, we propose real-time edge fault-tolerant SCADA (detection of anomalies) based on learning continuous sequential data for efficient control of the UAV's altitude and heading. Our data-driven solution, involving an extensive suite of sensory data processing, demonstrates the potential to significantly reduce communication and decision-making capabilities in cases of remote locations, enabling safer and more efficient UAV operations. The proposed system leverages machine learning algorithms to analyze real-time data from both extrinsic and intrinsic UAV sensors, allowing for predictive control and fault detection. By processing data at the edge, our solution reduces the need for bandwidth-intensive data transmission minimizing latency and ensuring swift and reliable decision-making. We show the data collection and training in a high-fidelity aviation simulator that closely matches real flight conditions.

articleTitle: Embedded KETOS Deep Learning Classifier for the AIOS Buoy
abstract: The Acoustic Intelligent Ocean Surveillance (AIOS) buoy is an autonomous Passive Acoustic Monitoring (PAM) system that encompasses acoustic data collection, embedded deep learning classifier models, and a buoyancy compensation capability (allowing it to move up and down in the water column under its own control), The current prototype uses as many commercial off the shelf (COTS) components so that each component can be integrated, tested, and independently improved before completing a complete integrated system design. The current AIOS buoy architecture separates functional components into physically distinct modules. This approach allows separately investigating energy requirements for each module. This discussion focuses on the energy required to operate the Ketos deep learning classifier within the current AIOS buoy architecture.

articleTitle: Optimization of an Open-Source Based Turbidity Sensor for Deep-Sea Mining Application
abstract: This paper presents the optimization of an open-source-based turbidity sensor designed for monitoring turbidity in the context of deep-sea mining. The existing sensor exhibits an insufficiently low sensitivity in low turbidity ranges and is based on an overly complex manufacturing method. To address these issues, the sensor's transmitted light measurement is augmented with a scattering light measurement, leading to improved resolution and sensitivity. Furthermore the general design is enhanced to simplify production and improve reproducibility. The optimized sensor is subsequently evaluated through a series of tests, including calibration procedures, signal stability assessments, and pressure tank experiments. As a result, the optimized sensor shows significantly higher sensitivity in the low turbidity ranges, making it a valuable tool for precise turbidity measurement in deep-sea environments.

articleTitle: A Whale Sanctuary in Nova Scotia: A Multidisciplinary and Multicultural Effort
abstract: A growing body of scientific evidence demonstrates that dolphins and whales (i.e., cetaceans) experience poor welfare when confined to concrete tanks in entertainment parks. Whereas most captive cetaceans cannot survive if released directly into the ocean a viable alternative is to transfer them from tanks to authentic sanctuaries. An authentic cetacean sanctuary is a place that provides a combination of a complex, natural environment continuous with the ocean and human care. Key to wildlife sanctuaries is the promotion of autonomy and giving back as much as one can of what was taken from its residents. In this presentation we describe the Whale Sanctuary Project (WSP), the world's first cetacean sanctuary effort for both captive beluga whales and orcas. Founded in 2016, WSP is a non-profit organization representing a groundbreaking collaboration among scientists, engineers, dolphin and whale advocates, legal experts, and many others. Its mission is to create a sanctuary for captive orcas and beluga whales in Canada and aid other cetacean sanctuary efforts globally. The WSP is preparing a 100-acre site on the eastern shore of Nova Scotia to welcome whales in 2025. Herein we describe the sanctuary site, highlight and update some of the milestones and challenges WSP has met over the years as the sanctuary progresses towards completion. We also discuss the importance of local community encouragement and participation for such a project as well as engagement with First Nations, who share the goal of rectifying our relationship with the ocean and the animals who live in it.

articleTitle: Optimizing Bathymetric Data Collection Campaigns Using Processed Water Quality and Depth Data from Multispectral Satellite Imagery
abstract: Planning for Airborne Lidar Bathymetry (ALB) campaigns can benefit from knowledge of water clarity conditions of the intended survey area. Analysis of a historical time series of water clarity data to optimize Lidar penetration can assist to determine the most effective time for the survey campaign. This Water Quality (WQ) time series is extracted from satellite-derived data recorded by high resolution multispectral satellites. As the volume of spatio-temporal data produced from multiple sensors over a 30+year archived dataset can be overwhelming, a simple webapp is introduced to assist visualization and analysis. This article shows the methods of WQ analysis using high resolution satellite sensors, the webapp and how it benefits ALB survey campaigns, namely in the reduction of project risks and increased efficiency. Additionally, we highlight Satellite-Derived Bathymetry (SDB) technology as a supplemental tool to serve mapping and monitoring of shallow water zones globally. Like WQ, SDB requires scientific data analysis and a scalable and standardized IT infrastructure. We introduce SDB-Online as such a solution enabling the spatial mapping and monitoring of bathymetry and how it adds value to ALB and other survey methods.

articleTitle: Autonomous Control of Seafloor Data Transfer from Lander Edokko Mark-I to AUV Hobalin
abstract: In this study, a long-term, wide-area seafloor monitoring method was tested in coastal sea area by combining a seafloor landing probe (lander) and a hovering AUV (H-AUV). The lander and the H-AUV performed direct acoustic communication and acoustic positioning on the seafloor autonomously, and the H-AUV approached the lander in a horizontally opposed position for the underwater optical wireless communication. This established underwater high-speed LAN communication and enabled the transfer of large-capacity video data on the lander to the research vessel via the H-AUV.

articleTitle: Cooperative docking system for Unmanned Surface Vehicle (USV)
abstract: Unmanned Surface Vehicles (USVs) offer diverse applications, from security missions to oceanographic surveys. A major challenge in USV autonomy is the development of effective docking systems to ensure operators remain out of the water. This paper introduces a novel docking solution based on a cooperative approach that enhances USV autonomy by enabling autonomous return to docking stations. This docking approach utilizes a combination of sensors, including GPS RTK with dual antennas and IMUs, along with secure wireless communication between the USV and the docking system. This configuration ensures the system is independent of weather conditions. The focus is on the architecture of this system and the management of path planning using an Artificial Potential Field (APF) algorithm. Initial results from simulations are presented, followed by experimental studies conducted in a lake, demonstrating the system's robust performance.

articleTitle: An Adaptive Acoustic Transceiver Testbed on System-on-Chip for Underwater Communication
abstract: This paper describes a test setup to support the development of a bi-directional acoustic communication link relying on adaptive transceivers. The physical layer relies on the JANUS protocol for discovery of new nodes and assessment of the channel conditions. The transmitter has a bandwidth of 5 kHz at a center frequency of 27.5 kHz, while the receiver relies on broadband hydrophones. The embedded system allows to transmit in diverse underwater scenarios, and the System-on-Chip is programmed to transmit various waveforms including through coded Orthogonal Frequency Division Multiplexing (OFDM). Key elements of the program are described to maintain real-time operation on the embedded systems. At the receiver, the data is sampled at 96 kHz and a 4 Mbps cabled link to a host interface is developed to diagnose the communication link reliability.

articleTitle: Observations of Baleen Whale Vocalizations in the New England Offshore Wind Lease Area from August 2023 to July 2024 Using Multiple High Resolution, Bottom-Mounted Hydrophone Arrays
abstract: Three high-resolution, 32-channel, linear hydrophone arrays coupled with real-time, autonomous baleen whale detector-classifiers were deployed on the ocean floor in the New England offshore wind lease area from August 2023 to March 2024. The purpose of the deployment was to monitor the construction area transit lanes for vocalizations from baleen whales, in particular North Atlantic right whales (NARW) and humpback whales. The hydrophone arrays were monitored in real time by human analysts with the assistance of an autonomous classifier, with real-time data transmitted to an on-shore command-and-control facility. During the deployment period, over 8,500 autonomous detection-classifications of NARW (n=2500) and humpback (n=6050) whales were recorded. The majority of detections occurred during the month of February, with about 2,000 NARW calls recorded in the first week of February alone. The NARW diel pattern shows that vocalizing whales are most active at dusk and near midnight, consistent with others historical measurements. Multiple periods of pile driving operations noise were also recorded and analyzed. Right and humpback whale detection ranges exceeding 15 nautical miles were confirmed via multi-system cross-fix localization when the same whale is detected on two or more arrays, including a few examples of multi-system localizations observed during pile driving in June 2024.

articleTitle: Enhancing Fish Detection and Classification in Sonar Images Through Deep Learning
abstract: To ensure the preservation of a robust ecosystem and healthy fish populations, it is necessary that we carefully monitor the number and presence of different fish species. In this article, we fine-tuned and tested an automated real-time state-of-the-art deep learning model YOLOV9. We showed that an adaptation of the widely used YOLO deep learning model can accurately detect and classify eight species of fish from a public DIDSON imaging sonar dataset captured from the Ocqueoc River in Michigan, USA. Our results demonstrate that deep learning models can be used to detect and classify fish using high resolution imaging sonar. We obtained a high score with a mean Average Precision of 0.894 for YOLOv9-e and 0.871 for YOLOv8xl (mAP:50).

articleTitle: Volumetric Gradient-Aware Methodology for the Exploration of Foreign Objects in the Seabed
abstract: The underwater domain presents a myriad of challenges for perception systems that must be overcome to achieve accurate object detection and recognition. To augment the performance and safety of existing solutions for intricate O&M (Operations and Maintenance) procedures, AUVs must perceive the surroundings and locate potential objects of interest based on the perceived information. A depth gradient methodology is employed to survey the seabed using a multibeam sonar to perform a coarse reconstruction of the scenario that it later used to locate and identify foreign objects. This could include rocks, debris, wreckage, or other objects that may pose potential exploratory interest. First results show that the proposed method was able to detect 100 % of the objects present in the scenario with an average chamfer distance error of 0.0238m between models and respective reconstruction.

articleTitle: Data Transportation Across Clusters of Distributed Underwater Acoustic Sensor Networks
abstract: This work explores the discovery of gateway agents to facilitate the transportation of data across clusters of distributed, surface denied, underwater acoustic sensor networks along an underwater acoustic backbone network to a centralized access point with surface access. The gateway discovery protocols presented herein demonstrate methods to allow agents to become self-aware of their role in the network and partition the backbone network from the underwater acoustic sensor network clusters in a kite-like graph topology; a topology that is used in the practice of connecting surface denied sensor clusters to a multi-modal access point. A naive and improved protocol for gateway discovery is presented and the benefits and computational cost are discussed.

articleTitle: An Empirical Analysis of the Impact of Scale in Bedforms Segmentation from Digital Bathymetric Models
abstract: Underwater dunes are the result of sediment transportation due to relatively strong or large-scale sustained flows. They can be associated with different hydrodynamical factors (i.e. grain size, flow velocity, tidal regime, etc.) and be present in different marine environments, such as deltas, estuaries, river channels, and shallow marine environments. Different approaches have been proposed in the literature to segment and characterize dunes aiming to reduce the ambiguity associated with the extraction of these structures from DBM allowing rigorous and repeatable extraction of these bedforms. Despite the success of these approaches, major challenges persist to further improve their performance. This manuscript focuses on analyzing the morphological classification of the seafloor that allows the identification of underwater dunes from a modelled seafloor surface.

articleTitle: Bathymetry Estimation using Machine Learning Techniques from Airborne Remote Sensing RGB Image Data
abstract: The intertidal zones of the Wadden Sea and estuaries are highly dynamic natural environments subject to constant spatial and temporal fluctuations. This study presents an innovative method for bathymetry estimation based on airborne RGB remote sensing imagery. Traditional acoustic in-situ measurements, while highly accurate, are limited by high costs and restricted accessibility. Our approach investigates color gradients and wave structures of the water surface using a k-means classifier to correlate optical properties with water depths. Additionally, surface waves are analyzed through two-dimensional Fourier transformation to extract wavelength and orientation. Initial results demonstrate a strong correlation between classified image data and reference bathymetric data, highlighting the suitability of this method for rapid and large-scale mapping of dynamic coastal areas. This technique provides a complementary tool to conventional methods, effectively capturing and documenting rapid changes such as sediment shifts and sandbank formation.

articleTitle: Development of Environmental Reproduction and Visualization Systems for Deep Sea Methane Hydrate Environment
abstract: As part of the research and development of shallow methane hydrate recovery and production technologies for deep-sea environments, the potential use of membrane structures for capturing methane seeps while mining and for pollution prevention to reduce environmental impact of mining has been investigated. This study has two principal objectives. The first is to gain insight into the degradation characteristics of the membrane materials that will be employed in the methane hydrate environment in deep sea. A further objective is to gain insight into the behavior of methane bubbles with a hydrate film on their surface, which differ from normal methane bubbles in their interaction with membrane materials. This includes the process of bouncing, deformation, sliding, fixation, and aggregation occur. These knowledges will be employed in the design of membrane structures for the production of methane hydrate in the deep sea. Novel systems that reproduce the methane hydrate environment on the seafloor in a laboratory have been developed. They consist of an environmental test system and a visualization system. This paper describes the design of the systems and presents some results obtained using the developed systems.

articleTitle: Quantification of the Effects of Preprocessing Filters on the Performance of GNSS-R Based Sea Ice Detection
abstract: This study examines the influence of preprocessing techniques on the performance of Global Navigation Satellite System Reflectometry (GNSS-R) based sea ice detection. Preprocessing techniques evaluated in this study include precipitation screening and SNR thresholding. SNR thresholds are tested with −3dB, 0 dB, +3 dB, and no threshold configurations. Precipitation screening is tested in three scenarios, containing all data, precipitation free data, and only precipitation contaminated data. Performance impact is determined by recording the sea ice detection accuracy, precision, and recall using the preprocessed datasets. The binary classification is conducted using two models: a histogram thresholding approach and a Bayesian approach. From these tests it was found that the inclusion of precipitation contaminated data did not result in an appreciable change to classification accuracy, precision, or recall. For SNR thresholding, classifcation accuracy peaks for the histogram thresholding approach when a SNR threshold of −3dB or 0 dB is applied. For the Bayesian approach, peak accuracy is achieved with a −3 dB threshold. These results indicate that an SNR threshold of < 0 dB results in superior classification accuracy and that precipitation may be considered negligible for sea ice detection purposes.

articleTitle: Air-Sea Surface Heat Fluxes in the Arabian Gulf: Insights from High Resolution Regional Ocean Model
abstract: The turbulent and radiative heat flux exchanges between the ocean and atmosphere play crucial roles in the earth's climate system. This study aims to quantify these air-sea interactive fluxes of the Arabian Gulf using a high-resolution regional ocean model MITgcm called MODEL-ERASHYC. The net heat fluxes from the model, three observation/satellite prod-ucts, and four annual mean climatology fluxes are compared. The MODEL-ERASHYC annual net heat flux shows the most negligible bias from climatology, while all the datasets closely resemble statistical parameters. Further latent, sensible, short wave and long wave radiative heat fluxes were calculated from the model, and it was observed that there is a net gain of 8 <tex xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">$W/m^{2}$</tex> heat to the gulf exhibiting a strong seasonality.

articleTitle: Rutgers-MTS Glider Technology Workshop - A Hands-On Experiential Learning Workshop on Slocum Gliders and an Opportunity for Workforce Development and Microcredential Certificates
abstract: Marine Technology Society is developing a series of Ocean Technician Microcredentials to facilitate both traditional and alternate routes to the Blue Economy workforce. This Microcredential plan consists of skillset tiers for various oceanographic technologies, including autonomous underwater vehicles. Ocean gliders are autonomous underwater vehicles used for an array of science and research applications, such as climate change, tropical storm intensification and model data assimilation, water quality and ocean acidification, and fisheries management. Gliders allow for safe, affordable, and around-the-clock data collection and can be deployed inexpensively, for months at a time in a variety of ocean conditions. Rutgers University Center for Ocean Observing Leadership and the Marine Technology Society host a week-long hands-on workshop on underwater glider technologies each June. Participants are introduced to the Teledyne Webb Slocum glider through experiential learning opportunities including preparing, ballasting, deploying, and piloting the glider. The workshop maximizes the active learning for all participants, while also ensuring comprehension of the essential basics applicable to Slocum gliders and many other AUVs. The goal of the workshop is for participants to gain an introductory knowledge of and justification for underwater glider principles and their associated science applications that can be built upon in future experiences. This workshop's authentic, introductory approach to AUV s, specifically Slocum gliders, fundamentally aligns with MTS's ocean technician microcredential plan at the Foundational tier for a Glider Trainee, meant for core knowledge and experience relevant to the specific technologies. The seamless overlap between MTS's endeavor and RUCOOL's Glider Workshop benefits all participants by providing assessed certification of participant skill and knowledge that will accelerate employment in the New Blue Economy.

articleTitle: Analyzing Sources of Inaccuracy in Ocean Surface Current Estimation from Shipborne Marine X-Band Radar Data
abstract: The extraction of sea surface current from marine X-band radar data significantly affects subsequent oceanic parameter determination. Therefore, assessing the influence of diverse factors on the accuracy of current parameter estimation is critical. In this paper, motion compensation is used to optimize the current estimation results derived by the Polar Current Shell (PCS) and the normalized scalar product (NSP) algorithms. The data collected by Defence Research and Development Canada between November 24 and December 5, 2008 was used for analysis. Root Mean Square Deviation (RMSD) and correlation analysis results for both current speed and direction obtained by PCS and NSP are presented. This study explores the intricate relations between measurement errors and precipitation, wind speed, vessel speed, vessel speed change and heading change. Our analysis indicates that the accuracy of current measurement significantly decreases under precipitation and lower wind speed conditions.

articleTitle: Re-Imagining Deep Sea Imaging Systems: Combining 4K Imaging with a Novel Web Client Interface to Create an Ultra-Low Latency, Live Video Streaming and Control Environment with Integrated Support for Real-Time Remote Operations and Outreach
abstract: In the rapidly evolving landscape of subsea imaging technologies, this paper describes the development of a versatile deep-sea imaging control system with an integrated web client interface for camera and device control. The imaging control system combines commercial of F-the-shelf components with a purpose-built server and custom software to produce a highly-scalable system capable of capturing geotagged still images and 4K video coupled with real-time companion metadata. Intended for applications requiring real-time operations, the imaging control system includes an ultra-low latency, live video streaming, interactive web client user interface combined with modular system architecture to facilitate adaptability and enable the opportunity to expand real-time remote operations and outreach across a range of submersible platforms and applications.

articleTitle: Learning Autonomous Docking Operation of Fully Actuated Autonomous Surface Vessel from Expert data
abstract: This paper presents an approach for autonomous docking of a fully actuated autonomous surface vessel using expert demonstration data. We frame the docking problem as an imitation learning task and employ inverse reinforcement learning (IRL) to learn a reward function from expert trajectories. A two-stage neural network architecture is implemented to incorporate both environmental context from sensors and vehicle kinematics into the reward function. The learned reward is then used with a motion planner to generate docking trajectories. Experiments in simulation demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach in producing human-like docking behaviors across different environmental configurations.

articleTitle: Power Breakers for Control and Monitoring Subsea Cabled Observatory Instruments
abstract: Subsea cabled observatory is a multidisciplinary research platform, there are variety instruments connecting observatory, whose power consumption vary from a few watts to a few hundreds watts. Those instruments power supply status require to be carefully remotely controlled and monitored. The basic parameters include controlling instrument on and off, monitoring instrument power supply health status such as voltage, current and ground fault etc., those data are critical for both properly instrument operating and data quality control. Ocean networks Canada (ONC) is continuing to extend its NEPTUNE, VENUS and SMART OCEAN observatories and keep building new observatories. A compact generic power control and monitoring unit was designed and build to meet those requirements. The unit is small enough (120Lx75Wx15H mm) to fit inside most pressure house. This power breaker includes the following functions: •Power on/off •Voltage and current monitoring •Over/under voltage protection •Over current automatic shunt down •Ground fault monitoring •Soft start and Inrush current control •Physical isolation power supplies from instruments •External DC/DC convertor temperature monitoring and remote control •RS422/485 addressable for units in daisy chain It had been successfully used for variety projects such as ONC Smart Ocean project, STRAW A and B neutrino project, RCM regional circulation moorings, hydrophone Arrays. A customized junction boxes such as MISO project had been build base on this module.

articleTitle: Ship Data Clustering for Improved Fuel Efficiency Optimization Decision Support Systems
abstract: In this paper, we propose a hybrid clustering algorithm based on hierarchical clustering in combination with string clustering, similar to that used in clustering genetic sequences, to extract clusters of operational activities from ship data. After extracting clusters (n=9), the distribution and summary statistics of each cluster are compared to Canadian Coast Guard provided operational definitions to obtain context from the clusters. The clustered data is used as the input to a fuel flow prediction model, which will in turn form the basis of an on-board decision support system for marine vessels with the goal of reducing fuel consumption. Finally, we compare the results of fuel flow predictions with models trained on a) different clusters and b) the full dataset, to determine the usefulness of these clusters in improving the performance of a fuel-optimization decision support system for on-board marine vessel use.

articleTitle: Sea Trial of Acoustic Positioning of 10 Targets per Second
abstract: The authors are developing combined aerial and underwater drones to address the manpower shortage in Japan for inspecting and monitoring aging water area infrastructure and fishing facilities (fixed nets, fish preserves, etc.), An aerial drone transports an underwater drone from land, and after landing on the water, the underwater drone is deployed to perform monitoring tasks, controlled remotely from the land. The underwater drone's location is obtained using acoustic positioning. In the future, to efficiently monitor a large number of targets, it is anticipated that multiple underwater drones will be used simultaneously, and there will be scenarios where divers collaborate with the drones. To verify the performance of the acoustic positioning system for the combined aerial and underwater drones in locating multiple targets, the authors conducted sea area experiments. Positioning of 10 targets per second was confirmed using time-division multiplexing. The positioning error (standard deviation of detected coordinates) was less than 6 cm, demonstrating sufficiently high accuracy. Pingers were also attached to an underwater drone and divers, realizing their simultaneous positioning. In the future, the authors plan to attempt the simultaneous positioning of more targets by using code-division multiplexing as well.

articleTitle: Real Time Flow Sensing - Cylinder Wake Turbulence Measurements Using Piezoelectrics
abstract: Collecting fluid flow information typically requires expensive, intrusive, and technically complex instruments. This study investigates a cost-effective and minimally invasive method for measuring turbulent flow using a voltage-generating piezo- electric strip. Open channel tests were conducted with a slender, highly flexible membrane placed in the wake of a cylinder, allowing for non-intrusive flow measurement. The wakes behind two separate cylinder diameters (3.175 cm and 1.27 cm) were measured at varying Reynolds number and streamwise distances in the wake. Turbulent pressure fluctuations were converted to voltage outputs, and spectral analysis identified Karman vortex shedding modes and frequencies. By positioning the piezoelectric strip at various distances along the cylinder wake, results indicated that increasing the Reynolds number significantly impacts the piezoelectric voltage response when the strip is closer to the cylinder. Acoustic tests were also performed to assess any facility noise that could interfere with the piezoelectric readings. This low-cost and simple sensor presents a practical alternative to traditional methods for measuring turbulence in situations requiring immediate or low-fidelity feedback in fluid flow application.

articleTitle: The Persistent Smart Acoustic Profiler: Infinite Possibilities for Soundscape Monitoring
abstract: The Persistent Smart Acoustic Profiler combines advanced technologies to create a lightweight ocean soundscape monitoring platform with infinite endurance and near real-time reporting capability. While ocean soundscapes are crucial for understanding marine ecosystems and the behaviors of marine animals, they are severely undersampled and poorly understood. Numerous sensing strategies are being employed to add to the body of knowledge on soundscapes, however it is often both challenging and expensive to collect data over extended periods, especially in difficult-to-reach locations. With a variety of sensing tools at their disposal, scientists can monitor marine life, assess the health of ecosystems, and develop approaches that mitigate the impacts of anthropogenic sound, ultimately promoting a better coexistence between human activities and marine wildlife. PSAP offers a unique approach to soundscape monitoring. With its unlimited endurance, global communication capability and streamlined onboard signal processing, PSAP can be deployed once and never recovered, providing an endless stream of valuable soundscape information to shore in near real time from remote oceanic locations around the globe.

articleTitle: Background Clutter Modeling of Spatio-Temporal Sea Clutter Suppression for Low Grazing Angle X-Band Marine Radar
abstract: The electromagnetic wave emitted by radar radiates on the sea surface to form backscattering echo is defined as sea clutter. The performance of marine radar in target detection is significantly impacted by the sea clutter. The intensity of the spiky in data collected by high resolution radar with a low grazing angle results in a trailing phenomenon in the statistical distribution, which varies with changes in sea state and environmental conditions. To address the issue of unstable matching between the sea clutter distribution and the real background clutter distribution caused by spatiotemporal changes, a statistical modeling of background clutter in X-band high resolution and low grazing angle marine radar data with suppressing sea clutter. The objective of this paper is to identify the most suitable statistical distribution for the data, and to assess both the overall goodness of fit for the clutter probability density function (PDF) and the local fit for the tail region of the cumulative distribution function (CDF). The findings indicate that the KK distribution exhibits the highest overall goodness of fit, while the WW distribution demonstrates the best local fit in the tail region of the CDF distribution.
